name: Regime End Type
note: How current regime ended: coup/election/negotiation/collapse
why: Encodes the mechanism by which the previous regime fell (coup, election, negotiation, collapse), providing a baseline structural memory of institutional fragility that shapes how the current order may unravel. Regimes that replaced predecessors through coups or collapse face systematically higher recurrence risk for violent power transitions, making this a strong prior for political-violence and regime-change Trends.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage from 1900; coding relies on expert assessment so quality varies for pre-WWII and micro-states.

trends.reason: Prior coup-driven regime change is the single strongest structural predictor of coup recurrence; directly encodes the mechanism this Trend predicts.
Regimes that arrived via collapse or forced negotiation are more likely to over-centralise power as a survival strategy.
Transition type (negotiated vs. collapse) strongly conditions whether democratisation succeeds; orthogonal to the continuous V-Dem scores already in the pool.
Regime-collapse endings correlate with post-conflict power vacuums that seed insurgencies; adds path-dependence signal beyond current governance indices.

name: Armed forces personnel, total
note: Absolute military size; military power indicator
why: Absolute military size captures the coercive capacity of the state; rapid expansions or contractions signal rearmament, coup-preparedness, or fiscal strain that precede political ruptures. It provides a raw-power baseline that complements spending-ratio indicators already in the pool.
coverage_note: WB WDI sourced from IISS; reasonable coverage from 1985 onward, thinner for small states and fragile states pre-1990.

trends.reason: Military size trajectory is a first-order predictor of coup feasibility; large, growing armies correlate with coup attempts.
Military mobilisation patterns directly precede interstate conflict escalation and are a structural readiness signal.
Force size relative to population captures counterinsurgency capacity and predicts conflict duration.
Step changes in personnel levels often coincide with formal military reform events.

name: Mineral rents (% of GDP)
note: Mineral resource rents; extractive dependency
why: Mineral resource rents as a share of GDP captures extractive-sector dependency, which correlates with Dutch disease dynamics, elite capture, and boom-bust fiscal cycles that precede regime instability and conflict. Countries with high mineral rents but weak institutions are particularly prone to resource-curse trajectories that QGI Trends in political violence, coup, and economic crisis should detect.
coverage_note: Good global coverage via WB WDI; mineral-poor countries report near-zero rather than missing, so effective coverage is high; some small island states and microstates may be absent.

trends.reason: Resource wealth concentrated in state hands creates coup incentives; literature strongly links mineral rents to coup risk, especially in sub-Saharan Africa and MENA.
Greed-grievance models (Collier-Hoeffler) use mineral rents as a primary predictor; lootable resources fund insurgencies and prolong conflict.
Direct theoretical link — resource conflict Trend is almost definitionally tied to mineral rent levels; likely a top-feature candidate.
High mineral rents attract nationalization episodes as governments seek to capture resource revenue; Angola, Venezuela, Bolivia case patterns.
Mineral-dependent states facing governance crises are sanction targets (e.g., DRC, Zimbabwe), but the link is indirect and mediated by governance variables already in pool.

name: Manufacturing, value added (annual % growth)
note: Manufacturing growth; industrialization pace
why: Manufacturing growth captures real-sector economic momentum; sharp contractions precede recession events and fuel social unrest via job losses and industrial hollowing. It complements GDP-level signals with a sector-specific pace measure that responds faster to external shocks and trade disruptions.
coverage_note: WB WDI; broad coverage but thin for small/fragile states and some MENA; data gaps common pre-1980 for lower-income countries.

trends.reason: Manufacturing contraction is a leading indicator of recession; likely to crack the greedy top-40 for this Trend and enter top features.
Positive manufacturing growth is a canonical recovery signal; model should capture the directional swing from contraction to expansion.
Industrial contraction correlates with layoffs and labor unrest; plausibly cracks top-40 in countries where manufacturing is a large sector.
Policy interventions often follow or precede manufacturing trend reversals; medium signal strength in economies with active industrial strategy.
Prolonged manufacturing decline deepens inequality but the relationship is indirect and lagged; marginal lift expected.

name: CPIA public sector management and institutions cluster average (1=low to 6=high)
note: Public institution quality; state capacity composite
why: This composite CPIA score captures state capacity across public financial management, procurement, revenue mobilisation, and transparency — the institutional backbone that either contains or amplifies political shocks. Weak public-sector management is a structural precondition for fiscal crises, corruption spirals, and governance breakdowns that precede multiple instability event types.
coverage_note: IDA-eligible and blend countries only (~75 countries); excludes all IBRD-only middle- and high-income countries, so sample is heavily skewed toward fragile/low-income states.

trends.reason: Public-sector management quality is the single most direct institutional measure of corruption-enabling conditions; strong theoretical and empirical link to corruption event trajectories.
PFM sub-component directly measures budget process quality; deteriorations precede fiscal stress and austerity-driven policy changes.
Low state-capacity scores correlate with regimes substituting coercion for service delivery legitimacy; plausible top-40 entry.
Poor public institutions amplify recession severity and lengthen recovery; secondary economic signal.
Institutional failure can catalyse protest but the link is diffuse and mediated by many intervening variables.

name: Academic Freedom Index
note: Academic freedom: research, teaching, autonomy, campus safety
why: Academic freedom captures the early erosion of intellectual and scientific autonomy that typically precedes broader authoritarian consolidation; its suppression signals a government tightening ideological control over society. In QGI context, declining academic freedom co-moves with press censorship and civil society crackdowns, providing an upstream governance-quality signal before political violence or repression events manifest.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage from 1900; expert-coded estimates become thinner before ~1950 for smaller states but post-1970 data is robust for ~180 countries.

trends.reason: Academic freedom decline is a canonical early indicator of political repression; strong theoretical and empirical directional alignment.
Autocratizing executives systematically attack university autonomy as part of power consolidation; strong leading signal.
Transitions (in both directions) co-move with academic freedom changes; useful but collinear with other V-Dem indices already in pool.
Academic persecution (arrests, dismissals) is a measurable form of rights violation; plausible but partial overlap with broader civil-liberties indices.

name: Cereal imports (metric tonnes)
note: Volume of cereal imports; food import dependency and price shock vulnerability.
why: Cereal import volumes capture structural food-import dependency and vulnerability to global commodity price shocks — countries heavily reliant on external grain are acutely exposed when export bans or freight disruptions hit, making this a structural supply-side risk signal distinct from price-anomaly indicators already in the pool.
coverage_note: FAOSTAT Supply Utilization Accounts; near-universal coverage from 1961; small island micro-states and some early-1960s newly-independent states have gaps.

trends.reason: Cereal import dependency directly amplifies famine risk when global supply contracts; high-import-reliant countries face acute shortfall on supply shocks.
Food import shocks are a documented trigger of humanitarian emergencies; the volume signal captures supply-side exposure independently of price.
Food price spikes transmitted via import dependency are a primary trigger of bread-price protests; import volume is a plausible upstream predictor.
Import-dependent food systems concentrate cost shocks on lower-income households, amplifying inequality crises when global prices spike.
Large cereal-importing nations are more likely to be affected by food trade disputes, but the link to specific dispute events is indirect.

name: Equality Before Law and Individual Liberty Index
note: V-Dem v2xcl_rol — country-year political indicator
why: Captures how consistently a state applies law equally and protects individual liberties — deterioration precedes regime crackdowns, political repression episodes, and mass protest cycles. As a composite rule-of-law signal it provides a slow-moving but high-signal baseline that cross-validates faster V-Dem indicators already in the pool.
coverage_note: Near-universal V-Dem coverage from 1900; pre-1950 data thinner for small states; contemporary coverage essentially complete.

trends.reason: Rule-of-law collapse is a structural precursor to state repression; index captures the erosion arc directly.
Individual liberty sub-dimension directly indexes the conditions that define human-rights violation events.
Legal equality scores shift significantly around transitions; adds signal distinct from electoral V-Dem components.
Perceived inequality before law is a documented grievance driver for large-scale protest mobilisation.

name: Real interest rate (%)
note: Real lending cost; investment incentive measure
why: Real interest rate captures the actual cost of capital after inflation, signalling investment incentive collapse or financial repression that often precedes capital flight, banking stress, and currency pressure. Sharp negative swings distinguish deliberate monetary loosening from inflation-driven erosion, both of which load onto economic instability Trends.
coverage_note: Coverage improves post-1990; many low-income countries lack consistent series; volatile outlier years (hyperinflation episodes) may need capping before use.

trends.reason: Real interest rate collapses or extreme spikes are canonical precursors to exchange-rate crises; directly maps to the canonical movement shape.
Negative real rates erode bank margins and fuel credit bubbles; this series is a primary banking-fragility leading indicator.
Tight real rates choke investment; the pre-recession tightening trajectory is a well-established signal.
The series is the direct output of central bank policy; shifts cleanly encode both tightening and easing episodes.
Interest rate environment shapes borrowing cost for governments, providing marginal orthogonal context to fiscal events.

name: CPIA average (IDA resource allocation index)
note: Composite IDA country policy assessment; governance quality
why: The IDA CPIA composite captures policy and institutional quality across 16 dimensions — fiscal management, debt policy, governance, social inclusion — making it a strong lagging signal of state fragility and the structural conditions that precede fiscal crises, political repression, and coups. Countries with deteriorating CPIA scores systematically exhibit governance erosion trajectories that precede destabilisation events by 1-3 years.
coverage_note: IDA-eligible countries only (~75); excludes IBRD-only and high-income states; scores available annually from 2005.

trends.reason: CPIA governance cluster tracks accountability and rule-of-law erosion that structurally precedes executive consolidation episodes.
CPIA public-sector cluster directly scores transparency and anti-corruption frameworks — low scores indicate environments where corruption events cluster.
Fiscal management sub-score within CPIA anticipates disruptive fiscal policy shifts in fragile states.
Social protection and equity sub-scores capture structural under-investment that drives inequality crises.

name: Property Rights Index
note: V-Dem v2xcl_prpty — country-year political indicator
why: Weak property rights signal deteriorating rule of law and elite predation, conditions that historically precede political crises, mass protest, and institutional collapse. As a V-Dem expert-survey index it captures the subjective reality that citizens and investors face, not just formal legal text.
coverage_note: Near-universal V-Dem coverage from 1900; post-WWII country expansion means most countries from 1945+; very sparse for microstates pre-1970.

trends.reason: Property rights erosion is a direct structural correlate of corruption regimes; strong theoretical and empirical link.
Property rights contraction reliably precedes and accompanies power consolidation; captures the legal dismantling step.
Declining property rights accompany the crackdown environment but are partially redundant with other civil-liberties V-Dem signals.
Land seizures, expropriation, and property insecurity motivate protest mobilization especially in middle-income countries.
Tangential via investment-chilling effect; economic channels captured more directly by growth/credit variables.

name: Bribery incidence (% of firms experiencing at least one bribe payment request)
note: Business bribery rate; corruption direct measure
why: Direct firm-level measure of corruption friction — when bribe demands on businesses spike, it signals eroding state legitimacy and weakens the economic conditions that precede political crisis. Complements V-Dem corruption indices with a behavioural, survey-grounded signal rather than expert assessment.
coverage_note: Enterprise Survey coverage is irregular — roughly 3-5-year gaps per country; concentrated in lower-middle-income and IDA countries; many high-income and small-island states absent.

trends.reason: Firm-level bribery is the most direct behavioural proxy for the corruption deterioration that precedes and accompanies this Trend's canonical shape.
Rising bribery burdens raise operating costs and deter investment, contributing to the economic slowdown pattern.
High bribery rates co-occur with weak rule of law environments where repression is more likely.
Corruption grievances are a noted protest mobilisation trigger but this indicator is survey-based with long lags, limiting temporal precision.

name: Refugee Recognition Rate (derived: recognized / total decisions, annual)
note: Share of decided claims that receive refugee status; internationally accepted measure of origin-country threat level
why: High refugee recognition rates signal that receiving countries accept the origin country as genuinely dangerous, providing an internationally-adjudicated, externally-validated measure of persecution or conflict severity. This is distinct from raw refugee counts — it captures legitimacy of threat, making it a clean instability signal with low reporting-bias.
coverage_note: Only countries with meaningful asylum claim volumes produce stable rates; very small origin countries have high variance from small denominators; coverage improves markedly post-2000.

trends.reason: Recognition rate spikes are near-contemporaneous with armed conflict escalation and credibly lead refugee stock indicators, giving the model an internationally-validated signal of conflict severity.

Persecution-based refugee status is specifically adjudicated on political/religious repression grounds, making recognition rate a quasi-independent cross-country measure of state repression intensity.
Countries with sustained high recognition rates systematically correlate with documented human rights abuses; adds external validation orthogonal to V-Dem expert scores.
Most directly aligned trend — recognition rate captures the legitimacy and international acceptance dimension of displacement flows, complementing stock/flow volume indicators.
Sub-threshold violence driving asylum claims without triggering full conflict coding; recognition rate picks up this grey zone.

name: Youth Bulge (Population 15-24, % Total)
note: Share of 15-24 year olds in total population; UN WPP via OWID; political instability risk signal
why: A high share of 15-24 year-olds creates a large pool of economically marginalized, politically activated youth — a robust cross-national predictor of mass mobilization and insurgency onset. It captures the structural demographic pressure that precedes protest waves, labor unrest, and recruitment into armed groups.
coverage_note: UN WPP via OWID; near-universal coverage including small states; projections extend to 2100 but historical series used.

trends.reason: Youth bulge is one of the most replicated structural correlates of protest mobilization; strong prior for entering top features.
Large youth cohorts provide recruitment pool for insurgencies; well-established in conflict-onset literature.
Youth unemployment concentration amplifies industrial unrest; mediating variable but plausible top-40 entry.
Youth bulge strains education/labor absorption, feeding inequality crises; orthogonal signal from income measures.
Demographic pressure correlates with sub-threshold political violence episodes; plausible contributor alongside conflict indicators.

name: SDG 6.4.2 Level of water stress — freshwater withdrawal as % of available freshwater (%)
note: Water stress ratio; agricultural water security and conflict risk from scarcity.
why: Water stress (freshwater withdrawal as % of available freshwater) is a structural scarcity signal that drives agricultural failure, resource competition between communities, and regime-destabilizing food insecurity; it is particularly predictive in arid and semi-arid regions where marginal scarcity translates rapidly into political pressure. As a slowly-evolving structural variable it captures multi-year run-up shapes that QGI Trends in drought, humanitarian crisis, and resource conflict should detect.
coverage_note: FAOSTAT SDG 6.4.2 coverage is uneven: ~170 countries reported but many only have data for benchmark years (2015, 2017, 2020) rather than annual series; interpolation common; small island states and microstates often absent.

trends.reason: Water stress is the structural precondition for drought vulnerability; high baseline stress amplifies the impact of rainfall anomalies into famine trajectories.
Near-definitional link — water crisis Trend is directly indexed to withdrawal-vs-availability ratios; almost certain top-feature candidate for this Trend.
Inter-community and inter-state resource conflicts frequently center on water; Nile, Tigris-Euphrates, Indus basin disputes fit this Trend's pattern.
Chronic water stress feeds into humanitarian deterioration by undermining food production and displacing populations; useful structural covariate.
Water scarcity is a recognized environmental migration driver but the signal is slow-moving and heavily mediated by agricultural and economic channels already captured elsewhere.

name: Domestic credit to private sector (% of GDP)
note: Credit depth; financial development and leverage
why: Private credit depth captures financial leverage and the degree of banking system intermediation; rapid credit expansions are among the strongest known predictors of banking and currency crises, while prolonged contraction signals deflationary stress. The series directly captures the financial-system amplification channel central to economic-stress Trends.
coverage_note: WB WDI; one of the broadest financial series; minor gaps for conflict-affected and sanctioned states in early decades.

trends.reason: Credit booms and busts are textbook banking-crisis predictors; this series directly captures the pre-crisis leverage build-up and is very likely a top-40 entry.
Excessive private credit fuels capital-flow vulnerabilities and FX pressures that culminate in currency crises; consistently appears in crisis literature.
Credit-cycle downturns amplify recessions; negative credit growth flags contraction risk, though recession has many concurrent drivers.
Liberalization events are often accompanied by financial deepening and credit expansion; plausible top-40 entrant for this Trend.
Post-crisis credit collapse forces emergency fiscal responses; tangential upstream signal with indirect causal path.

name: Informal employment rate by sex (%)
note: Share of employed in informal arrangements; instability, social protection deficit proxy
why: Informal employment rate reflects the share of the workforce outside social protection and stable labour contracts — a structural vulnerability that depresses resilience to economic shocks and fuels grievance-based mobilisation. High informality is both a poverty trap signal and a governance-quality indicator, directly relevant to social unrest and economic crisis event types.
coverage_note: ILO modelled estimates extend coverage to ~130 countries but with varying data quality; early years before 2005 are sparse for many countries; high-income OECD countries have near-complete coverage while low-income coverage relies heavily on modelling.

trends.reason: Informality-driven precarity and social protection exclusion are canonical grievance conditions underpinning protest waves; likely top-40 entry for this Trend.
Informal employment rate defines the boundary of organised labour; spikes in formal-sector insecurity and transitions into informality directly precipitate strikes and lockouts.
Informality is a core structural cause of persistent poverty and wage inequality; strong causal and empirical pathway.
High informality limits automatic stabilisers during downturns, amplifying recession depth; useful secondary feature.
Policy reforms targeting social protection and formalisation are often directly triggered by high informality levels.

name: Legislature Opposition Parties Operate Freely
note: Opposition parties operate freely in legislature
why: The ability of opposition parties to operate freely in the legislature is a direct measure of competitive political space; its contraction signals authoritarian drift and foreclosing of peaceful power-alternation channels. QGI uses this to detect pre-crisis governance deterioration before opposition suppression escalates into street politics or coup attempts.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-coded; reliable from ~1950+ for most countries; pre-1950 thinner but still broad; unicameral/no-legislature states coded accordingly.

trends.reason: Legislature opposition suppression is a definitional component of power consolidation; among the strongest institutional leading signals.
Opposition party freedom directly tracks democratic transitions and reversals; expected strong AUC contribution for this Trend.
Coups are often preceded by legislative dysfunction and opposition suppression; directional but indirect signal.
Constraining opposition in legislature often coincides with broader repression campaigns; plausible top-40 candidate.

name: Rebel Group Territorial Demands Active (binary, country-year)
note: Binary: rebel groups with stated territorial/autonomy demands active; from UCDP Conflict Issues Dataset, secessionism signal
why: Flags active rebel groups making territorial or autonomy demands — a direct structural precursor to secessionist insurgencies and civil-war escalation distinct from battle-death intensity signals. It captures the presence of a mobilised challenger with an existential stake, which shapes both onset probability and conflict duration.
coverage_note: Coverage limited to countries with active UCDP-recorded conflict; zero-conflict countries coded implicitly 0 but must be derived; pre-1989 coverage thinner.

trends.reason: Territorial demand is a core incompatibility type in UCDP taxonomy; binary flag cleanly identifies the insurgency-prone structural state.
Autonomous-demand conflicts are the main driver of federalisation and devolution events; indicator is a near-direct cause signal.
Territorial demands often overlap with ethnic mobilisation; adds conflict-structure dimension not captured by death counts.
Secessionist conflicts attract external patron support and intervention; territorial-demand flag is a proxy for intervention risk.

name: Interest payments on external debt (% of GNI)
note: Interest payments relative to GNI
why: Interest payments on external debt as a share of GNI measure the fiscal burden of servicing foreign obligations, a leading signal of debt distress that typically precedes austerity, default risk, and the social unrest those trigger. It captures debt-service squeeze independently of stock levels, making it complementary to stock-based ratios.
coverage_note: Strongest coverage for developing economies with World Bank reporting obligations; rich OECD countries with market-financed debt may have gaps in early decades.

trends.reason: Rising debt-service burden is a classic precursor to currency crises as reserves are drained to service foreign obligations.
Debt-service crowding out of discretionary spending is the primary driver of austerity-type fiscal reforms; this series directly measures that pressure.
High interest payments reduce fiscal space for counter-cyclical spending, amplifying recession depth and duration.
Austerity triggered by debt-service pressure is a recurrent mobilising grievance; this series provides the upstream structural signal.
Sovereign debt stress often co-occurs with banking fragility, providing marginal complementary signal.

name: Interest payments (% of revenue)
note: Debt servicing share of revenue; fiscal stress
why: Interest payments as a share of government revenue directly measures fiscal distress: when debt service crowds out discretionary spending, governments face stark trade-offs between servicing creditors and funding services, creating the fiscal-social stress that precedes currency crises, austerity-driven protests, and regime-threatening fiscal collapses. This ratio is a core early-warning metric in sovereign debt analysis.
coverage_note: Coverage strong for emerging markets from 1995; sparser for low-income states pre-2000 and some small islands throughout.

trends.reason: High debt-service-to-revenue ratio is a canonical leading indicator of currency crises and IMF interventions.
Spiralling interest burden directly triggers austerity packages and emergency fiscal policy changes.
Fiscal squeeze from debt service compresses social spending, fuelling austerity protest movements.
Sovereign fiscal stress propagates to domestic banking systems via bond holdings and contingent liabilities.

name: Net barter terms of trade index (2000 = 100)
note: Export vs import price ratio; commodity terms of trade
why: Terms-of-trade shifts determine the real purchasing power of a country's exports and are a leading driver of fiscal stress, currency pressure, and social unrest in commodity-dependent states — exactly the macro shock profile preceding economic crises and political turbulence.
coverage_note: WB WDI coverage concentrated on goods-exporting economies; service-dominant and small-island states often missing; pre-1980 sparse.

trends.reason: ToT deterioration directly compresses foreign-exchange earnings, is a textbook currency-crisis precursor; strong causal channel.
Commodity ToT collapses are among the most reliable recession triggers for resource-exporting countries.
Revenue shortfalls from ToT decline force austerity or deficit spending; policy response often a data-visible event.
ToT-driven import price spikes translate to food/fuel cost-of-living pressure that fuels street mobilization.
Indirect pathway via economic grievance; signal is partially diluted by many intervening variables.

name: Liberal Component Index
note: V-Dem v2x_liberal — country-year political indicator
why: Aggregates constitutional constraints on executive power, rule of law, and individual liberties into a single latent score — captures the institutional erosion trajectory that precedes democratic backsliding, political repression, and mass mobilisation. Its continuous scale makes multi-year movement shapes learnable by XGBoost walks.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage; pre-1945 estimates rely on sparse historical coding and carry wider uncertainty intervals.

trends.reason: Declining liberal index is the canonical leading signal of executive power consolidation — directly measures the erosion of checks this Trend captures.
Liberal constraints breakdown directly precedes and enables systematic repression; strong theoretical and empirical alignment.
Rising liberal scores are the definitional signal of democratisation — a top feature candidate for this Trend's run-up shape.
Constitutional rewrites often coincide with liberal index inflections; contributes movement shape information.
Liberal erosion is a documented protest trigger; movement shape plausibly aligns with protest escalation window.

name: Executive Embezzlement and Theft
note: Executive embezzles public funds for private use
why: Executive embezzlement directly measures the diversion of public resources for private gain at the top of the political hierarchy — the most destabilizing form of corruption because it erodes fiscal capacity, signals impunity, and triggers elite defection and popular grievance simultaneously. It complements composite corruption indices by isolating executive-specific theft rather than averaging across institutions.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert survey coverage; early decades (pre-1950) thinner for smaller states but coverage is broad from 1970 onward.

trends.reason: Most directly aligned indicator — executive embezzlement is the core behavioral signal for the political corruption Trend and likely enters the greedy top features.
Embezzlement typically accelerates as executives consolidate power and eliminate institutional checks; captures the rent-extraction dimension of consolidation trajectories.
Coup literature consistently finds elite defection driven by executive corruption; embezzlement is a measurable precursor to loss of military/elite coalition loyalty.
Regimes engaged in embezzlement typically suppress accountability mechanisms, linking executive theft to broader repression patterns.

name: Ideology-Based Legitimation
note: Legitimacy based on official state ideology
why: Ideological legitimation measures how much a regime rests on a state ideology (Marxism, Islamism, nationalism) rather than democratic consent or personal loyalty — regimes with brittle ideological foundations face acute instability when that ideology loses credibility. This signal captures a distinct legitimacy pathway to regime crisis that is orthogonal to corruption or repression indices.
coverage_note: V-Dem standard coverage; expert-coded so some thin-state coverage is less reliable pre-1950.

trends.reason: Ideological legitimation is a classic consolidation tool; strongly discriminates regimes that centralize power under a state doctrine.
Ideological legitimacy collapse is a leading precursor to transition; distinct from election-based accountability signals.
Ideologically-driven regimes face loyalty fragility within the military when ideology is challenged; plausible top-40 entry.
Ideological delegitimation often triggers mass protest waves; adds a legitimacy-pathway signal distinct from economic grievance.
Ideological regimes tend toward repression but correlation with other repression indicators is high; marginal independent contribution.

name: Military Appointment Criteria (Merit vs. Loyalty)
note: Military officers appointed by merit, not political loyalty
why: Measures whether military officers are promoted on merit versus political loyalty — a key indicator of coup-proofing versus professionalism that determines how the armed forces respond to civilian authority in crises. Loyalty-based militaries simultaneously signal authoritarian consolidation and fragile civil-military relations prone to factional splits or coup plotting.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert coding; near-universal country coverage but early-period scores (pre-1950) carry higher uncertainty in many regions.

trends.reason: Merit-vs-loyalty appointment is a core structural determinant of coup risk; factional military rivalry emerges when loyalty overrides competence.
Military reform events are directly indexed by shifts in appointment criteria; this indicator likely leads the event.
Executives who purge merit-based officers and install loyalists are consolidating power; the two variables co-move but loyalty appointments may lead the visible consolidation.
Loyalty-appointed militaries are more willing tools of domestic repression; adds explanatory dimension beyond civilian judicial/police repression indicators.

name: Government-Perpetrated One-Sided Violence Active (binary, country-year)
note: Binary: government is perpetrator of one-sided violence against civilians; state repression / democide signal
why: This binary flags years when the state itself is the perpetrator of one-sided civilian killings, distinguishing regime-directed repression from battlefield violence — a critical distinction for predicting political crises, mass protest, and international intervention triggers. Its presence in a country-year sharply elevates the base rate of subsequent political ruptures.
coverage_note: UCDP one-sided violence dataset from 1989; only conflict-affected or repressive contexts contribute positives — large share of zeros for peaceful states is structurally meaningful.

trends.reason: Government-perpetrated killing is the definitional core event for political repression trends; near-certain top-feature candidate.
State-directed civilian deaths are among the most severe human rights violation signals in the pool.
State killing of civilians is a documented trigger for subsequent mass protest mobilisation.
International responses to atrocities (R2P invocations, no-fly zones) are preceded by government one-sided violence.

name: Refugees as Share of Origin Country Population (derived)
note: Refugees from country / total population; normalizes for country size, key comparability metric for ML features
why: Refugees as a share of origin country population is a population-normalized signal of the severity of push factors — persecution, conflict, or collapse — driving people to flee; it strips out country-size confounding and makes the underlying risk intensity comparable across all countries for ML feature engineering. Sustained increases in this ratio precede and accompany QGI Trends in political repression, civil war, and humanitarian crisis.
coverage_note: UNHCR refugee stock data by country of origin covers ~185 countries from 1990; denominator (population) from WB; countries with near-zero refugee outflows will show 0 rather than missing, so effective coverage is high.

trends.reason: Refugee outflow ratio is one of the strongest contemporaneous and lagged signals of civil war severity; Syria, Afghanistan, South Sudan exemplify the canonical pattern.
Persecution-driven flight is the direct causal chain behind refugee status recognition; high ratio strongly signals systematic repression against specific groups.
Mass refugee generation is both a consequence and reinforcer of humanitarian crises; normalized ratio captures crisis magnitude independent of country size.
Near-definitional top feature for this Trend; normalizing by population makes it the best cross-country comparator in the UNHCR family.
Refugee ratio captures systematic human rights failures that cause flight even when direct violence metrics are noisy or underreported.

name: Social Media Used to Organize Offline Violence
note: Social media used to coordinate real-world political violence
why: Directly measures the degree to which social media is used to coordinate real-world political violence, capturing a digital mobilization pathway absent from traditional indicators. Provides a near-contemporaneous signal of violence organization that can precede or accompany attacks, political violence events, and protest escalation.
coverage_note: V-Dem; global coverage but v2sm* social media items are only meaningful post-2000; reliable signal from ~2010 onward as social media penetration expanded globally.

trends.reason: Direct mechanistic link: social media coordination of offline violence is definitionally captured by this indicator — very likely top-40 entry for political violence Trend.
Social media mobilization underpins modern protest waves; overlaps substantially with organizing for collective action and protest escalation.
Online radicalization and coordination precede attacks; plausible top-40 entry, though not all terrorism is organized via mainstream social platforms.
Hate speech and incitement on social media fuel communal violence; captures the enabling digital environment for inter-group conflict.
Governments often respond to online-coordinated violence with repression; causal direction may weaken the signal but it is a plausible co-variate.

name: Workers involved in strikes and lockouts — total (thousands)
note: Total workers in strikes; breadth of industrial unrest
why: The breadth of strike participation (workers involved, not just event count) captures the scale of coordinated labour grievance and is a leading indicator of social tension that can escalate into broader political mobilisation. Unlike fatality-based signals, it detects institutional friction early, before violence thresholds are crossed.
coverage_note: Highly uneven: ILO administrative data depends on national labour ministries; many low-income countries lack consistent reporting; coverage effectively ~90 countries with usable series but sparse for sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia.

trends.reason: This is the definitional outcome metric for the Labor Action Trend; workers-in-strikes is the most direct empirical input and almost certain to be a top feature.
Large-scale strike mobilisation frequently co-occurs with or presages street protest waves; strong empirical cross-event correlation.
Regimes facing large worker mobilisations often escalate repression; strike breadth may lead repression onset by 1-2 years.
Major strike waves are often triggered by wage cuts and layoffs during recessions; bidirectional signal.
Strike activity is a lagging indicator of inequality but the causal link is indirect and the feature may not crack top-40 for this Trend.

name: Low pay rate by sex (%)
note: Share of workers earning below 2/3 of median wage; low-pay prevalence and inequality
why: A high share of workers earning below two-thirds of the median wage captures structural wage compression and labour-market precarity that fuels economic grievance and social unrest. In QGI models, low-pay prevalence is an orthogonal economic-stress signal distinct from unemployment rates, particularly useful for rich-country instability patterns where formal employment stays high but wage adequacy collapses.
coverage_note: ILOSTAT low-pay data requires labour force survey microdata; coverage skewed toward OECD/upper-middle income countries (~90); developing-country observations sparse and irregular, limiting ML utility for fragile-state Trends.

trends.reason: Low-pay prevalence is the primary economic grievance driver of strike waves and labour mobilisation; strong expected top-40 placement for this Trend.
Wage-adequacy grievances contribute to protest mobilisation especially where NEET and informal rates are also high; plausible but complementary to other social indicators.
Low-pay share directly measures the working-poor segment; relevant but coverage gaps in lower-income countries constrain this Trend's country pool.

name: Droughts, floods, extreme temperatures (% of population, average 1990-2009)
note: Climate disaster exposure; climate fragility baseline
why: This WB fixed decadal average (1990–2009) captures the share of a country's population historically exposed to droughts, floods, and extreme temperatures — a structural baseline for climate-related fragility that does not change year-to-year and is uncorrelated with annual fluctuations, adding independent structural variance as a static covariate.
coverage_note: Single fixed value per country (1990-2009 average from EM-DAT); treat as static covariate — year values reflect the measurement window, not an annual time series.

trends.reason: Percentage exposed to climate-related disasters is essentially a summary natural-disaster vulnerability index; expected to dominate this Trend's top-40.
Baseline drought/flood exposure is the structural precondition for drought-and-famine events; persistent top-feature as a static discriminator.
Historical flood exposure directly indexes structural flood-and-cyclone risk; strong baseline discriminator across countries.
Climate-exposed countries face higher baseline humanitarian crisis risk; static covariate adds structural differentiation independent of annual variation.
Climate hazard exposure is a documented structural driver of displacement and migration; informative for the pre-event structural context.

name: External debt stocks (% of exports of goods, services and primary income)
note: External debt vs export capacity; debt sustainability
why: External debt stock relative to export earnings is the canonical debt-sustainability ratio used by IMF/World Bank early-warning frameworks; it directly measures whether a country's capacity to generate foreign exchange can cover its foreign obligations. Trajectory shifts in this series reliably precede currency crises and sovereign restructuring events.
coverage_note: Good coverage for developing-economy borrowers; OECD high-income countries with bond-financed debt are patchier; early 1970s thin for many countries.

trends.reason: This ratio is the standard IMF debt-sustainability tripwire; crossing critical thresholds is among the strongest currency-crisis leading indicators in the empirical literature.
Sovereign over-indebtedness regularly triggers banking crises when debt is rolled through domestic banks; debt-to-exports deterioration leads both events.
IMF conditionality and creditor pressure triggered by high debt ratios typically force structural fiscal adjustment.
Heavily indebted countries under sanctions face compounded export contraction that worsens the ratio, providing marginal context.
Debt overhang suppresses investment and consumption, lengthening and deepening recessions.

name: Net lending (+) / net borrowing (-) (% of GDP)
note: Fiscal balance (net); primary/deficit signal
why: Net lending/borrowing (fiscal balance) as a share of GDP is the primary measure of the government's fiscal stance — a structural deficit trajectory signals accumulating debt burden and reduced capacity to absorb shocks, while sudden swings indicate policy-driven austerity or stimulus that reshapes the political economy. It is a near-universal leading macro variable in fragility frameworks.
coverage_note: Good coverage for OECD and most emerging markets; patchy for sub-Saharan Africa and fragile states pre-2000; some definitional inconsistencies across IMF/WB compilations.

trends.reason: Fiscal balance is the direct measure of the fiscal stance shift that defines fiscal policy change events.
Persistent deficits monetised by central banks are the textbook precursor to currency crises.
Collapsing revenue-driven deficit widening co-moves with recession onset and amplifies contractionary dynamics.
Austerity-driven deficit reduction programmes are a well-documented trigger of social unrest and protest mobilisation.

name: Current account balance (BoP, current US$)
note: Absolute current account balance; external position level
why: The current account balance in absolute USD captures the scale of a country's external financing gap or surplus, making it a direct precursor to balance-of-payments crises, IMF programme entry, currency devaluations, and associated political shocks that are disproportionately large in absolute-dollar terms for bigger economies.
coverage_note: Near-universal WB WDI coverage from ~1980; small island states and post-Soviet countries join from 1990/1992; absolute USD series can be noisy for dollarised economies.

trends.reason: Sustained large current-account deficits are the canonical BoP vulnerability signal that precedes currency crises.
Current account reversals often accompany sudden-stop financial crises and banking sector stress.
Abrupt CAB deterioration is a coincident-to-leading recession signal, especially for import-heavy economies.
Sanctions regimes visibly compress export receipts and shift the CAB; the absolute-USD series captures scale of impact.
CAB feeds fiscal narrative but the link is indirect; government revenue channels more directly covered by other fiscal indicators.

name: Personal remittances, received (% of GDP)
note: Remittance dependency; diaspora economy signal
why: Remittance inflows as a share of GDP reveal diaspora-dependency — high ratios signal fragile domestic labour markets and exposure to external income shocks, while sudden remittance collapses historically precede currency and fiscal stress in remittance-dependent states.
coverage_note: WB WDI series; good coverage from 1995 onward; early 1990s sparse for post-Soviet and small-island states; informal flows systematically undercounted in high-remittance countries.

trends.reason: Remittance collapse is a documented trigger of balance-of-payments stress; high dependency amplifies exchange-rate vulnerability preceding currency crises.
Remittance-dependent economies are especially exposed to global slowdowns; sudden drops translate directly into consumption and fiscal contractions.
High remittance ratios proxy large diaspora stocks, themselves a signal of prior or ongoing displacement pressure from origin countries.
Remittance dependency concentrates income gains in migrant households, structurally shaping inequality dynamics; marginal orthogonal signal.

name: Risk premium on lending (lending rate minus treasury bill rate, %)
note: Banking risk spread; credit market tightness
why: The risk premium on lending (lending rate minus T-bill rate) measures the spread between bank lending costs and the risk-free rate, capturing banking sector perceived credit risk and financial system stress in real time. When this spread widens sharply it signals deteriorating bank-borrower conditions that precede credit crunches, bank failures, and associated economic contractions.
coverage_note: WB WDI coverage is patchier than broader macroeconomic indicators — many low-income and transition economies lack T-bill markets; coverage strongest for middle-income and emerging market countries post-1990.

trends.reason: Risk premium is a near-real-time market signal of banking stress; spread widening reliably leads banking crisis onset and provides information distinct from balance-sheet NPL ratios.
Financial stress captured by lending spreads frequently co-moves with currency pressure episodes; adds a credit-channel signal to complement exchange rate and reserve indicators.
Credit tightening via elevated risk premium is a classic transmission mechanism from financial stress to broader economic contraction.
Spread dynamics partially reflect monetary policy regime shifts; marginal orthogonal signal relative to headline interest rate indicators.

name: Gross capital formation (annual % growth)
note: Investment growth momentum
why: Gross capital formation growth captures the investment pulse of an economy — sharp declines signal a confidence crisis, credit crunch, or political uncertainty feeding back into the real economy before recession indicators fully register. For QGI, it provides a leading-edge economic stress signal that can discriminate between structural decline and cyclical contractions preceding crisis events.
coverage_note: WB WDI standard; data sparse for some small states and conflict-affected countries in early decades; post-1980 coverage is broad.

trends.reason: Investment collapse is a direct component of recession dynamics; expected to rank highly in top-40 for this Trend.
Financial crises are preceded and reinforced by investment pullbacks; strong empirical link via credit-investment channel.
Sharp capital formation drops often coincide with or precede currency crises via confidence and FDI channels.
Public investment changes drive GCF swings; fiscal austerity cycles are reflected here, adding texture beyond revenue/deficit signals.
FDI is a sub-component of GCF; some overlap but total GCF adds domestic investment signal; marginal orthogonality.

name: Adjusted net savings, including particulate emission damage (% of GNI)
note: Genuine savings rate; long-run wealth sustainability
why: Adjusted net savings subtracts natural resource depletion and pollution damage from gross savings, capturing whether a country is genuinely building or drawing down its wealth — a long-run sustainability signal that leads fiscal crises and resource-curse dynamics. Chronic negative genuine savings predict the exhaustion of buffers that states rely on to absorb shocks without political destabilisation.
coverage_note: WB WDI coverage from ~1990; some small states and resource-rich countries have gaps where depletion estimates are uncertain.

trends.reason: Sustained negative genuine savings is a multi-year leading indicator of wealth erosion that precedes growth collapse; more forward-looking than GDP growth itself.
Governments facing genuine-savings deterioration are more likely to enact emergency fiscal shifts; the signal prefaces revenue or expenditure reform events.
Resource depletion embedded in the metric directly links to resource-rent exhaustion and the competition/conflict that follows; strong theoretical link.
Oil-dependent states show volatile genuine savings correlated with price cycles; the metric aggregates both oil wealth and its depletion cost in one signal.
Emission damage component adds a climate-policy-readiness signal but it is marginal compared to the fiscal and resource channels.

name: Diagonal Accountability Index
note: Civil society and media as accountability mechanism
why: Diagonal accountability captures the watchdog power of civil society and independent media to hold executives to account — a dimension orthogonal to formal institutional checks, and one that erodes measurably before autocratisation accelerates. Declining diagonal accountability predicts democratic backsliding and repression events with a multi-year lead.
coverage_note: V-Dem covers virtually all countries from 1900; pre-1945 estimates carry higher coding uncertainty.

trends.reason: Diagonal accountability erosion is a canonical leading indicator of executive power grabs documented across autocratisation episodes.
Repressive states systematically weaken civil society and media before and during repression campaigns.
Diagonal accountability levels distinguish genuine democratisation from facade transitions.
Media and civil society constraints reduce anti-corruption oversight, correlating with corruption event escalation.

name: Accountability Index
note: Overall accountability: vertical + horizontal + diagonal
why: V-Dem's Accountability Index aggregates vertical, horizontal, and diagonal accountability mechanisms, providing a comprehensive measure of whether state power faces institutional checks; declining accountability trajectories are a well-established precursor to executive power consolidation, democratic backsliding, and the removal of constraints that ultimately enable political repression and corruption. Its composite nature gives it broad coverage across many Trends compared to narrower sub-indices.
coverage_note: V-Dem covers ~180 countries from 1900; quality of expert codings is high for post-1945 but thinner for pre-1945 and some smaller states; recent years (2023-2024) may have preliminary scores.

trends.reason: Accountability erosion is the definitional mechanism of power consolidation; this index directly measures the institutional constraints being dismantled.
Transitions to and from democracy hinge on accountability rebuilding or collapse; the aggregate index captures multi-channel change that single-dimension measures miss.
Weak accountability is the structural enabler of corruption; the diagonal and horizontal sub-components (media, judiciary, legislature) are the watchdog mechanisms corruption erodes.
Repression typically follows accountability collapse; useful precursor signal especially in regimes transitioning from partial to closed autocracy.
Constitutional changes that weaken oversight bodies drive accountability scores down; the index tracks the institutional consequences of constitutional manipulation.

name: Number of Active State-Based Conflicts (country-year count)
note: Count of distinct state-based conflict dyads active in country-year; multi-front war complexity signal
why: Counts distinct active state-based conflict dyads per country-year, capturing multi-front war complexity that single binary active/inactive flags miss. A country fighting three simultaneous armed groups faces qualitatively different instability than one with a contained single insurgency, making this a unique structural signal.
coverage_note: UCDP; covers all states globally but non-zero values only for ~60-80 conflict-affected countries per year; zero-inflated distribution; complete coverage for active-conflict countries.

trends.reason: Count of active conflict dyads is a core measure of insurgency complexity and directly aligns with the civil war Trend's movement shape; near-certain top-40 entry.
Multiple concurrent state-based conflicts amplify overall political violence and reflect broader state-society breakdown.
Multiple simultaneous conflicts compound displacement, food insecurity, and civilian harm; plausible top-40 entry.
Complex multi-party conflict environments attract foreign intervention as external actors back different warring factions.
High conflict counts create demand for peace processes; the link is real but indirect and temporally delayed.

name: External Support to Conflict Parties (binary, from ESD dataset)
note: Binary: at least one warring party receiving external state support; internationalization and proxy-war signal
why: External state support to conflict parties converts internal conflicts into proxy wars, dramatically prolonging duration, raising lethality, and triggering foreign intervention — the presence of this binary flag distinguishes internationalised conflicts from purely domestic ones and is a strong predictor of escalation cascades. It captures the geopolitical dimension that purely domestic indicators miss.
coverage_note: Coverage conditional on conflict occurring; for non-conflict country-years the flag is 0 (informative absence); ESD dataset extends back to 1975 for relevant dyads but not all UCDP SB conflicts have coded external support.

trends.reason: External support is mechanistically upstream of foreign intervention escalation; this is the most direct available signal for this Trend and almost certain to be a top-5 feature.
Proxy-war dynamics sustain insurgencies that would otherwise collapse; external support is a strong duration and intensity predictor.
External support to conflict parties is a direct precursor path to interstate escalation when the supporting state becomes directly involved.
Internationalised conflicts with external sponsors frequently attract UN sanctions and arms embargoes against the supporting party or recipient.
External support often correlates with territorial-autonomy conflicts where a neighbouring state backs separatist rebels.

name: Refugees by Country of Asylum (total stock, end-year)
note: End-year stock of refugees hosted in each country; measures humanitarian burden and regional spillover
why: The stock of refugees hosted in a country captures the humanitarian burden placed on receiving states, including resource strain, social tension, and spillover from neighbouring conflicts that can destabilise host-country politics. For QGI, this is a regional-contagion signal: large refugee stocks indicate proximity to active conflicts and stretch state capacity in ways that precede domestic instability events.
coverage_note: UNHCR population statistics are near-universal; early decades (1951-1980) cover mainly Cold-War displacement cases; modern coverage from ~1990 is comprehensive with consistent methodology.

trends.reason: Country-of-asylum refugee stock is a direct input to the migration and refugees Trend; expected core feature.
Large refugee inflows stress host-country health, food, and shelter systems; strong empirical link to humanitarian crisis escalation.
Refugee presence can inflame inter-group tensions in host communities; plausible but context-dependent.
Mass refugee flows sometimes precede or accompany international intervention; tangential signal with low directional specificity.

name: New Asylum Applications by Country of Origin (annual flow)
note: Annual asylum claims originating from each country; push-factor signal reflecting persecution or conflict intensity
why: Annual asylum application flows by country of origin are a push-factor signal aggregating international judgements about persecution and conflict intensity — thousands of individuals simultaneously choosing to flee constitutes a distributed early-warning system sensitive to rapidly deteriorating governance and conflict conditions, capturing emerging crises before they appear in annual governance indices.
coverage_note: UNHCR POPSTATS near-universal; some micro-states and closed autocracies have structural underreporting, but coverage is very broad.

trends.reason: Asylum application flow from origin country is definitionally the upstream driver of this Trend; expects to be among the single strongest features.
Surge in asylum claims is a direct revealed-preference measure of repression intensity; strong leading signal for repression escalation.
Asylum claimants cite persecution and rights violations as legal basis; the flow aggregates international assessment of human rights conditions.
Insurgency-driven displacement produces large asylum outflows; correlated but with some lag relative to combat onset.
Mass asylum applications frequently coincide with broader humanitarian emergencies; plausible co-predictor.

name: Asylum Backlog Duration (pending stock / annual decisions, derived)
note: Implied years to clear pending asylum backlog at current decision rate; institutional capacity and rule-of-law proxy
why: Derived asylum-backlog duration (pending stock divided by annual decisions) is a rule-of-law and state-capacity proxy for destination countries — long backlogs signal overwhelmed judicial systems and governance strain while also reflecting sustained origin-country push-factor intensity that exceeds host-state processing bandwidth. It is analytically distinct from raw refugee counts.
coverage_note: Reliable derivation requires both pending stock and decisions data; coverage limited to ~85 receiving states with functioning asylum systems; thin pre-2000; derived field needs construction from raw UNHCR tables.

trends.reason: Backlog duration captures the structural absorption gap between refugee-flow intensity and host-state capacity, a key migration-crisis dynamic.
Sustained backlog in destination states may reflect politically-driven slowdowns in recognition for specific nationalities, signalling repression abroad.
High originating-country refugee pressure captured via backlog adds a continuous structural human-rights signal independent of event coding.

name: Working days lost through strikes and lockouts — total
note: Total working days lost; headline economic cost of industrial conflict
why: Working days lost through strikes measures the intensity and breadth of industrial action beyond simple strike counts, capturing the cumulative economic disruption of labour conflict and signalling deteriorating government-labour relations that precede broader social mobilisation. It is a lagging confirmatory signal of economic stress translating into organised collective action.
coverage_note: Coverage is sparse and uneven; many countries do not report consistently; series has long gaps especially in Africa and MENA; only ~80-100 countries have usable multi-year series.

trends.reason: Days lost is the primary quantitative measure of strike magnitude and is near-definitionally the target variable for the labor_action Trend.
Large-scale strike waves frequently escalate into or accompany mass protest movements; this series captures the organised labour precursor.
Strike intensity spikes during recessions as workers resist wage cuts and layoffs, providing a social-response signal correlated with economic downturns.
Governments that crack down on strikes suppress this series, making sharp declines after elevated periods a potential repression signal.

name: Trade union membership rate (union density) (%)
note: Share of employees in trade unions; worker bargaining power and social dialogue signal
why: Trade union density captures the organised bargaining power of workers: high and rising density gives labour movements the structural capacity to mount sustained collective action, while sharp declines can signal repression of worker rights or deindustrialisation shocks that redirect grievances into broader political mobilisation. It is a direct leading indicator of labour-action events and an upstream variable for mass protest.
coverage_note: ILOSTAT administrative and survey data; sparse for informal-economy-heavy sub-Saharan and South Asian countries; reporting gaps create uneven time series.

trends.reason: Union density is the most direct structural predictor of strike capacity — high density enables the sustained mobilisation that produces labor action events.
Strong union networks provide organisational infrastructure for mass protest movements beyond narrow labour demands.
Union density shapes the political economy of welfare-state reform — high density countries face stronger resistance to retrenchment.
Suppression of union rights often accompanies broader political repression; declining density under autocratisation is a marginal signal.

name: Multidimensional Poverty Index
note: Composite index of acute poverty across health, education, and living standards; 0-1 scale from household surveys
why: The Multidimensional Poverty Index captures the acute deprivation that conventional income measures miss — poor health, low education, and inadequate living standards simultaneously — providing a structural fragility baseline that predicts the susceptibility of a population to mobilization under stress events.
coverage_note: Coverage limited to low- and lower-middle-income countries where household surveys exist; high-income OECD countries absent; irregular survey rounds mean time series has gaps (often 3-5 year intervals, not annual).

trends.reason: MPI is the definitional measure of multidimensional poverty; directly models the state this Trend event describes.
High MPI countries are overwhelmingly the sites of humanitarian crises; strong baseline fragility signal.
Accumulated deprivation lowers the threshold for grievance-driven protest mobilization under trigger shocks.
MPI's food/health components directly overlap with famine vulnerability; high-MPI populations have lowest coping capacity.
Structural deprivation feeds insurgent recruitment but MPI is slow-moving vs. the dynamic conflict variables.

name: Core Civil Society Index
note: Core civil society: organizational freedom, participation, consultation
why: Core Civil Society Index measures the organisational health and autonomy of civil society — its decline is a leading indicator of political closure and repression, while high levels predict mobilisation capacity for democratic transitions and mass protests; captures a dimension not fully reflected in electoral or institutional indices.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage; pre-WWII estimates rely on thin expert codings; post-1990 series most reliable for ML training.

trends.reason: Civil society suppression is both a mechanism and signal of political repression — declining CCSI traces the canonical run-up shape for this Trend.
Strong civil society is a robust predictor and enabler of successful democratic transitions; rising CCSI is a key leading signal.
Civil society organisational capacity determines protest mobilisation potential; CCSI captures the enabling environment for this Trend.
Executives consolidating power systematically curtail civil society; co-movement provides complementary signal to other V-Dem governance indicators.
Civil society suppression accompanies and enables human rights violations; moderate orthogonal contribution alongside CCSI sub-components.

name: Regimes of the World — Ambiguous Cases
note: V-Dem v2x_regime_amb — country-year political indicator
why: The Regimes of the World Ambiguous Cases indicator flags countries in hybrid or borderline regime categories — the exact zone where regime transitions are most likely to occur in either direction. Ambiguous regimes have the highest variance in near-term political trajectory, making this a leading signal for both democratization and autocratization events.
coverage_note: V-Dem coverage from 1900; broad cross-national coverage; the ambiguous-case coding is conceptually sparse in years with clear regime types but precisely targeted when it fires.

trends.reason: Ambiguous regime status directly flags the transitional zone where democratic transitions originate; fires reliably in the run-up windows of historical transitions.
Hybrid regimes with ambiguous legitimacy are the modal setting for coup attempts; ambiguous coding captures the institutional fragility that enables coups.
Autocratization often begins in ambiguous regimes where formal democratic institutions exist but norms are weak; signals the entry point for consolidation trajectories.
Ambiguous regimes typically hold contested or flawed elections; the indicator fires around election-related instability windows.
Constitutional changes are common tools for resolving or entrenching regime ambiguity; modest marginal signal beyond direct regime-change indicators.

name: Compliance with Judiciary
note: V-Dem v2jucomp — country-year political indicator
why: Compliance with judiciary measures whether executive actors actually abide by court rulings — a low score indicates that formal judicial checks have been hollowed out, revealing a regime willing to override institutional constraints. This captures a leading indicator of rule-of-law breakdown that precedes repression escalation, constitutional crises, and authoritarian consolidation.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-coded; standard global coverage; reliability improves post-1950 as expert pools densify.

trends.reason: Non-compliance with courts is a primary mechanism of power consolidation; expected strong top-40 entry.
Judicial non-compliance enables repression with impunity; strong causal prior and distinct from civil liberties indices.
Constitutional rewrites often accompany or follow executive defiance of courts; mechanistically linked.
Judicial non-compliance histories create transitional justice demands post-regime change; plausible leading signal.
Institutions that ignore court rulings enable human rights abuses; adds accountability-channel signal to abuse indices.

name: Judicial Purges
note: Politically-motivated removal of judges
why: Captures politically-motivated removals of judges, a low-frequency but high-salience event that directly measures executive encroachment on judicial independence and serves as a leading indicator for broader democratic backsliding. Judicial purges tend to cluster before executive power consolidation events and constitute a concrete, measurable precursor distinguishable from gradual de-institutionalisation.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-scored; global coverage with higher score uncertainty in early decades and micro-states.

trends.reason: Judicial purge is a canonical mechanism of consolidation — dismantling check institutions before expanding executive authority; strong leading indicator.
Removing independent judges removes the institutional barrier to arbitrary detention, trials, and repression; directly enables the event category.
Constitutional rewrites often follow or accompany judicial purges to lock in new power arrangements; purge timing may lead the formal constitutional event.
Purges in transition contexts signal failed or reversed accountability mechanisms; tangential but adds post-conflict institution-building signal.

name: Engagement in Independent Trade Unions
note: V-Dem v2catrauni — country-year political indicator
why: Independent trade union engagement measures the organisational infrastructure of civil society outside formal political channels; suppression of unions is an early governance stress indicator that also proxies for the social mobilisation capacity underpinning labour actions and mass protests. It captures a dimension of political competition not fully reflected in electoral indicators.
coverage_note: V-Dem full panel; coverage strongest post-1945; pre-1945 labour context harder to code for some regions.

trends.reason: Trade union organisational freedom directly determines the capacity and frequency of strike and labour action events.
Strong independent unions provide logistical backbone for mass protest coalitions beyond purely labour grievances.
Crackdowns on unions often accompany broader repression campaigns; union suppression is a repression leading indicator.
Organised labour pressure shapes social policy bargaining; union strength is a partial predictor of reform momentum.

name: One-Sided Violence Deaths — Best Estimate (country-year aggregate)
note: Best-estimate civilian fatalities from one-sided violence aggregated to country-year; targeted killing and atrocity intensity
why: One-sided violence deaths aggregate civilian fatalities from deliberate targeting by organized actors (governments and non-state groups alike), capturing state atrocity and militia killing that battlefield metrics miss; this directly measures the severity of political violence against unarmed populations, a key signal for Trends in repression, humanitarian crisis, and civil conflict escalation. Its country-year aggregation makes it ready for QGI's feature pipeline without further transformation.
coverage_note: UCDP GED/OS covers ~150 conflict-affected countries from 1989; countries with zero one-sided violence have missing or zero records — coverage is event-conditional, not universal; peaceful high-income countries will show zeros/NAs.

trends.reason: Government one-sided violence is the most direct empirical proxy for state repression intensity; targets civilian populations precisely to suppress political opposition.
OS deaths co-occur with and escalate during insurgencies; civilian targeting often intensifies as counter-insurgency strategies shift to attrition.
Mass civilian killing is among the most severe human rights violations; this metric captures the lethal extreme of the rights-abuse spectrum.
One-sided violence triggers displacement and aid access denial, escalating humanitarian deterioration; useful severity signal alongside displacement metrics.
Non-state one-sided violence frequently occurs along ethnic/communal lines (e.g., militias targeting minorities); aggregating both actor types captures this pattern.

name: State-Based War Intensity Flag (≥1000 deaths, binary, country-year)
note: Binary: state-based conflict reaches 'war' threshold (≥1,000 battle deaths); from incompatibility coding in PRIO-ACD dataset
why: Binary flag for state-based conflict reaching war threshold (≥1,000 battle deaths), distinguishing low-level armed conflict from full-scale war. This threshold crossing historically correlates with regime change, mass displacement, and external intervention events — marking the qualitative escalation that reshapes political trajectories.
coverage_note: UCDP/PRIO-ACD; same coverage as SB conflict series; binary variable so zero-inflated; all active-conflict countries captured with consistent threshold coding.

trends.reason: War-intensity threshold is the definitional ceiling of civil war severity; highest prior for top-40 entry in this Trend.
Interstate wars almost always cross the war threshold; binary flag will be near-perfectly predictive for active war years.
War-level violence drives mass displacement and refugee flows; plausible top-40 entrant for migration/refugee Trends.
War-intensity conflicts historically attract foreign military involvement, either to support a side or impose a ceasefire.
Full-scale war raises military salience and can trigger coups, but causation is contested and the signal is weaker than direct political indicators.

name: Coercive State Capacity (Hanson & Sigman)
note: Sub-dimension: government control of territory and monopoly on legitimate force; 177 countries 1960-2015
why: The Hanson-Sigman coercive state capacity sub-dimension measures a government's control over territory and monopoly on the legitimate use of force — the foundational prerequisite for conflict suppression and public order. It captures state fragility specifically on the coercion axis, distinct from extractive or administrative capacity, providing unique predictive value for conflict-related Trends.
coverage_note: Hanson-Sigman dataset ends 2015; no updates planned — treat as a structural slow-moving baseline covariate; increasingly stale for post-2015 windows.

trends.reason: Coercive capacity directly governs whether the state can suppress insurgencies; low scores are a well-validated conflict onset predictor.
Coercive capacity fragmentation (competing armed actors) is a structural coup prerequisite; this dimension captures that fragmentation.
Both very low (state too weak to repress) and moderate (state resorting to force) scores correlate with repression events through different mechanisms.
Weak territorial control enables communal militias to operate; coercive capacity is a plausible structural discriminator.
Inability to control territory correlates with disputed zones being actively contested; the sub-dimension is a proximate structural measure.

name: Mean surface temperature change on land (degrees C vs 1951-1980 baseline)
note: Country-level temperature anomaly (1961-2025); climate change exposure and agricultural risk.
why: Country-level land surface temperature anomaly is a direct measure of climate-change exposure that underpins agricultural yield shocks, food-price spikes, and water scarcity — pathways established in the conflict-climate literature as intermediate steps toward political instability. Including it gives the pool a slow-moving exogenous structural driver orthogonal to all governance and economic signals.
coverage_note: FAOSTAT temperature-change series covers virtually all countries from 1961 with annual updates; baseline period 1951-1980; small island states occasionally missing.

trends.reason: Temperature anomaly is the primary physical driver of droughts; directly predicts arid-zone yield failures that precede famine events.
Climate stress amplifies competition over scarce land and water; temperature anomaly is the best available proxy for this structural pressure.
Elevated temperature anomaly increases evapotranspiration and reduces surface-water availability, the core physical driver of water crises.
Multi-year temperature anomalies compound into food insecurity and displacement that define humanitarian emergencies, especially in semi-arid regions.
Climate-driven displacement is a growing but still secondary driver relative to conflict; temperature anomaly adds a marginal orthogonal signal.

name: Prevalence of undernourishment (PoU)
note: % population with chronic dietary energy deficit; SDG 2.1.1 anchor indicator; stability pillar of food security.
why: Prevalence of undernourishment (PoU) is the SDG 2.1.1 anchor indicator measuring the share of the population with chronic dietary energy deficit, providing the most direct quantitative signal of food security failure that underlies political instability, mass protest, and humanitarian crises. Rising PoU reliably precedes food-driven unrest and increases vulnerability to drought-famine events.
coverage_note: Annual estimates from 2001; pre-2001 data are available for some countries as 3-year averages but are less comparable; FAOSTAT reports 3-year rolling averages which smooth year-to-year variance.

trends.reason: PoU is the primary chronic food insecurity signal; elevated baseline or rising trend directly precedes famine events and is the canonical ingredient of drought-famine Trend models.
Undernourishment is a core component of humanitarian crisis severity; the series captures deteriorating food access independently of acute shock triggers.
Food price shocks combined with high baseline undernourishment are a well-documented driver of protest mobilisation; PoU captures structural vulnerability to food-price grievances.
Chronic undernourishment is one of the strongest single indicators of extreme poverty; co-movement with the poverty-inequality crisis Trend is high.
Food insecurity is a significant push factor for migration; provides marginal displacement-prediction signal alongside conflict indicators.

name: Prevalence of severe food insecurity (FIES)
note: % population with severe food insecurity only (sub-indicator of FIES suite); access pillar proxy.
why: The FIES severe food insecurity rate (% unable to eat for a day or more due to lack of resources) captures the most acute end of household food deprivation — the direct material deprivation channel linking food system failures to political instability, since populations facing starvation-level food access become highly sensitised to price shocks and government failures that trigger protests and violence.
coverage_note: FIES survey data from 2014; shorter time series than PoU; coverage broadened post-2016 via Gallup World Poll integration; pre-2014 imputed values available but modelled.

trends.reason: Severe FIES rate directly measures the acute food deprivation that defines famine conditions and precedes famine event declarations.
Acute food insecurity is a core trigger and indicator of humanitarian crises requiring international response.
Severe food insecurity historically correlates with food-price protest mobilisation; the 2008 and 2011 food crisis protest waves are canonical examples.
Severe food insecurity is a headline deprivation outcome that defines poverty crises in low-income settings.
Acute food insecurity is a documented driver of distress migration and refugee flows, especially when combined with conflict.

name: State Territorial Control
note: Full territorial control; no warlords or rebel-held areas
why: State territorial control is a foundational fragility signal — when governments lose effective control over parts of their territory to warlords or rebels, it directly precedes or accompanies civil conflict escalation, insurgency, and humanitarian crises; captures a state-failure dimension distinct from institutional quality indices.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal; pre-1945 codings estimated from historical sources with wider uncertainty; post-1989 most reliable for conflict-focused Trends.
