trends.reason: Territorial control loss is both a cause and effect of insurgency — the sharpest available signal for this Trend's onset and escalation shape.
Territorial fragmentation triggers displacement and access denial; strong leading signal for humanitarian deterioration.
Territorial control erosion often precedes military intervention as armies act to restore order; plausible top-40 feature.
External actors intervene when host governments lose territorial control; provides movement shape signal for this Trend.
Ungoverned spaces enable communal group clashes; territorial control is a plausible contributory feature.

name: International Autonomy (Degree of External Constraint)
note: International constraints on government autonomy
why: International Autonomy measures the degree to which a government operates free from external constraints — low autonomy signals dependency relationships, conditionality, or foreign domination that fundamentally alter political risk dynamics. Countries with low autonomy are structurally exposed to foreign intervention, externally-induced regime change, and sanctions-driven instability.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert survey; good coverage from 1945 onward; colonial-era coding less reliable for very small or administered territories.

trends.reason: Low international autonomy is the direct structural condition enabling foreign intervention; this indicator captures the target country's vulnerability, making it likely to enter greedy top features for this Trend.
Countries with low autonomy are disproportionately sanction targets or dependent on patron states that impose conditionality; autonomy captures the power asymmetry sanctions exploit.
Low-autonomy states enter asymmetric bilateral treaties under external pressure; the indicator signals the structural dependence context in which treaty events occur.
Peacekeeping missions are overwhelmingly deployed in low-autonomy states where external actors can project force or conditionality; captures host-state receptivity.
Externally-backed coups are a subset of coups; low autonomy slightly elevates coup probability via patron-client dynamics but the effect is secondary.

name: Military expenditure (% of central government expenditure)
note: Military share of govt spending; resource allocation
why: Military expenditure as a share of central government spending measures the degree to which the state prioritises coercive capacity over civilian services — a structural signal for both internal security preoccupation and resource trade-offs that erode public goods provision. High and rising military shares can precede coup risk (praetorian states) or reflect pre-conflict arms build-ups.
coverage_note: WB WDI from 1988 (SIPRI-sourced); some states have multi-year gaps due to unreported or classified budgets.

trends.reason: Praetorian budget capture — high military spending share reflects institutional power that correlates with coup propensity in civil-military theory.
Government-expenditure military share captures fiscal commitment to war-fighting capacity beyond GDP share; strong link to inter-state conflict build-up.
Budget share shifts are a direct measurable signal of military policy change events — rearmament, drawdown, or force restructuring.
Counter-insurgency campaigns show up as rising expenditure share; elevated baseline also signals institutional militarisation that precedes civil conflict.

name: Extractive State Capacity (Hanson & Sigman)
note: Sub-dimension: government ability to raise sustainable revenues (tax+non-tax); 177 countries 1960-2015
why: Extractive state capacity — the government's ability to raise sustained revenues — is a foundational determinant of fiscal resilience, public goods provision, and regime stability; states that cannot tax reliably are far more vulnerable to fiscal crises, foreign-debt spirals, and popular delegitimisation. It is theoretically distinct from administrative or coercive capacity and adds non-redundant signal.
coverage_note: Hanson & Sigman dataset ends at 2015; post-2015 gap limits near-term predictive window unless complemented by WB tax-revenue indicators.

trends.reason: Revenue-raising capacity sets the structural ceiling for fiscal policy; low extractive capacity predicts austerity-forced policy shifts.
Governments with weak extractive capacity cannot backstop financial systems, raising sovereign-bank nexus vulnerability.
Low fiscal capacity limits counter-cyclical response, deepening and lengthening recessions.
Revenue-starved states sometimes resort to coercive rent extraction in lieu of legitimate taxation.

name: Public Sector Corruption Index
note: Public sector corruption in service delivery
why: V-Dem's Public Sector Corruption Index aggregates expert-coded corruption in service delivery, public sector procurement, and judiciary — moving beyond perceptions to coded observable behaviours across 180 countries since 1900. It captures the institutional degradation pathway through which corruption erodes state legitimacy, triggering protest, fiscal crises, and democratic backsliding.
coverage_note: V-Dem standard coverage; near-universal for post-1945; pre-1945 estimates have wider confidence intervals. For QGI the effective window is 1970-2024 given recipe length requirements.

trends.reason: This is the definitional signal for the Corruption Trend; public-sector corruption index is the most direct and comprehensive available measure and near-certain to dominate the greedy selection.
Anti-corruption protest is one of the most common mass-mobilisation triggers globally; the public-sector dimension is particularly salient for service-delivery grievances.
Corruption is both a cause of democratic breakdown and a target of reform; the index captures both corruption-driven erosion and reform-driven improvement trajectories.
Executive power grabs are frequently enabled by and accompanied by expanding public-sector corruption as patronage networks are built.
Corrupt judicial and security institutions are enablers of human rights violations; secondary pathway signal.

name: Regime Corruption Index
note: V-Dem v2xnp_regcorr — country-year political indicator
why: The Regime Corruption Index captures systemic corruption embedded in regime maintenance — through patronage, vote-buying, and state capture — rather than incidental misconduct, making it a structural measure of governance decay that destabilises regimes over the medium term. QGI uses this to distinguish corruptly entrenched regimes (high stability illusion, sudden collapse risk) from rule-of-law deterioration that manifests through institutional indicators.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-coded; very broad coverage; note this index captures regime-level corruption specifically, not general public sector corruption (covered separately by v2x_pubcorr).

trends.reason: Regime Corruption Index is among the most directly matched indicators for the political corruption Trend; expected core feature.
Anti-corruption grievances are a primary mass-protest driver; regime corruption levels predict protest mobilisation well empirically.
Power consolidation and regime corruption co-evolve as executives use corrupt networks to entrench; plausible but partial overlap with other V-Dem measures.
Corruption levels affect both the probability and direction of democratic transitions; useful contextual feature.

name: Clientelism Index
note: Clientelism: vote buying, patron-client linkages, particularism
why: The V-Dem Clientelism Index measures vote buying, patron-client linkages, and particularism in political exchange — the degree to which political competition operates through selective benefit distribution rather than programmatic policy. Clientelism is a structural enabler of corruption cycles, election fraud, and regime durability that is distinct from corruption indices alone, capturing the organizational logic through which resources are extracted and distributed.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage from 1900; expert-coded with good developing-country representation; modern period (post-1970) most reliable.

trends.reason: Clientelism is the organizational machinery of political corruption; expected to be among the top structural features for this Trend.
Vote buying and patron-client electoral mobilization are definitionally election-related phenomena; strong mechanistic link to electoral fraud and contestation events.
Clientelistic regimes entrench executive power by co-opting potential opposition through selective distribution; plausible structural antecedent.
High clientelism correlates with protest events when excluded groups lose patron-network access or when networks visibly collapse under fiscal stress.
Clientelism levels predict the difficulty and trajectory of democratic transitions; well-supported structural feature in the democratization literature.

name: Regime Duration (Years in Power)
note: Years of current regime; longer = more entrenched/stable
why: Regime duration captures the entrenchment of the current political order — very short durations flag fragile newly-established regimes prone to early collapse, while very long durations signal ossified systems at risk of sudden legitimacy collapse or succession crisis. This non-linear signal complements continuous governance-quality indexes by encoding regime-lifecycle position.
coverage_note: Full V-Dem coverage from 1900; regime-end and restart dates validated by expert coders; near-complete for all sovereign states.

trends.reason: Coup probability peaks at both very short durations (unstable new regimes) and after very long autocratic tenures; duration encodes this non-linear risk.
Transitions cluster around regime exhaustion after long autocratic periods or at vulnerable early stages; duration is a direct lifecycle position signal.
Mid-to-long duration regimes consolidate power incrementally; duration trend predicts the consolidation arc better than a single-year snapshot.
Constitutional rewrites cluster at regime-transition boundaries and during long-regime consolidation phases, both captured by duration.

name: Autocratization Episode (binary, ERT)
note: Whether country is in an ongoing autocratization episode; V-Dem Episodes of Regime Transformation; regime change signal
why: The V-Dem ERT Autocratization Episode binary flag directly identifies countries in active processes of democratic erosion, making it one of the most theory-aligned predictors of executive power consolidation, political repression, and eventual regime change. As a binary state variable it provides a crisp switching signal that complements continuous V-Dem indices.
coverage_note: Coverage follows V-Dem country-year scope (~180 countries from 1900); ERT episodes are well-validated from ~1974 onward (Third Wave democracies); pre-1974 episode coding is thinner.

trends.reason: Autocratization episodes are near-definitionally the process by which executives consolidate power; this binary flag is the most direct predictor of this Trend.
Autocratization episodes often terminate in either full authoritarian consolidation or regime collapse and democratisation; the flag marks the transition risk window.
Repression of civil society, media, and opposition is the primary mechanism through which autocratization progresses; the episode flag correlates strongly with repression events.
Autocratization frequently proceeds through constitutional manipulation; the episode flag predicts constitution-altering events within the episode window.
Failed or incomplete autocratization can trigger military intervention; the flag captures elevated coup risk during democratic backsliding.

name: Government-Perpetrated Civilian Deaths Best Estimate (one-sided, country-year)
note: Fatalities from government one-sided violence; state atrocity magnitude, distinct from battlefield deaths
why: Government-perpetrated one-sided civilian killings measure the intensity of state atrocity — a qualitatively distinct signal from battlefield deaths that indicates a regime is targeting its own population, which systematically precedes mass refugee flows, foreign intervention triggers, and international sanctions. Magnitude of state killing is a strong discriminator between ordinary repression and catastrophic violence trajectories.
coverage_note: UCDP OSV dataset covers all conflict-affected contexts ≥25 deaths/year threshold; zero-coded for non-atrocity country-years; reliable from 1989.

trends.reason: Government civilian killings are the highest-intensity manifestation of political repression and directly define this trend's most predictable precursor.
State atrocity deaths are the most severe human rights violations measurable quantitatively at country-year level.
Mass government atrocity is a primary trigger for R2P-framed foreign military interventions.
State killing campaigns drive displacement flows as targeted populations flee; correlated with refugee stock build-ups.
One-sided government violence often co-occurs with or escalates into full civil war; the atrocity signal leads insurgency intensification.

name: IDPs as Share of Country Population (derived)
note: UNHCR IDP stock / total population; normalized internal displacement burden, comparability-adjusted
why: UNHCR's IDP stock normalized by population provides a governance-sourced view of internal displacement intensity that complements IDMC's figure — when both series agree, confidence in the displacement signal increases; divergence flags data quality issues for quality-control in the ML pipeline.
coverage_note: UNHCR IDP stock is limited to countries where UNHCR has operational presence and a mandate; coverage far narrower than IDMC (~80 countries vs 150+); significantly correlated with IDMC_CONF_STOCK_POP so feature collinearity is a concern.

trends.reason: Captures displacement at the high end of the severity spectrum where UNHCR has declared its mandate; valid conflict intensity signal.
UNHCR's mandate-based IDP coverage is specifically for the most severe humanitarian crisis contexts.
IDP pressure precedes and correlates with cross-border refugee movements; normalised ratio improves cross-country comparability.
UNHCR IDP presence implies repression in many cases but the series is too narrow geographically to be a primary signal.
UNHCR presence correlates with peace operations but adds little marginal signal beyond conflict and humanitarian variables.

name: Total Forcibly Displaced (refugees + asylum-seekers + IDPs, derived)
note: Aggregate forced displacement burden for a country; single composite signal for ML feature engineering
why: Aggregate forced displacement (refugees + asylum-seekers + IDPs) provides a composite headline measure of the cumulative human cost of instability — its multi-year trajectory captures both conflict intensity and state failure duration in a single ML-ready feature, with strong predictive signal for humanitarian and conflict Trends.
coverage_note: UNHCR annual data; pre-2000 IDP estimates less systematic; derived composite requires consistent sub-series availability; small-island states may have near-zero values creating structural zeros.

trends.reason: Total forced displacement is the aggregate outcome variable for humanitarian crises — cumulative stock captures crisis duration and intensity together.
Displacement magnitude tracks conflict intensity closely; the composite aggregates multiple UNHCR signals into a single high-signal feature.
Directly measures the phenomenon this Trend captures; most likely to enter greedy top features for this recipe.
State repression generates refugee and asylum flows; composite stock reflects cumulative persecution pressure.
High displacement levels trigger peacekeeping deployments; stock trajectory aligns with pre-agreement escalation shape.

name: Prevalence of moderate or severe food insecurity (FIES)
note: % population experiencing moderate/severe food insecurity per Food Insecurity Experience Scale; SDG 2.1.2.
why: The FIES moderate-or-severe food insecurity prevalence captures the share of population experiencing meaningful dietary access gaps, bridging the gap between mild food stress and outright famine — the band where food-driven social unrest and political grievance are most likely to emerge. It is demand-side, survey-based, and captures income shocks faster than production-side agricultural indicators.
coverage_note: FIES suite only available from 2014 when FAO began the global rollout; coverage improving annually but short time series limits historical backfill; partial coverage in high-income countries (low relevance).

trends.reason: Most directly aligned — moderate/severe food insecurity prevalence is the early-warning population-level signal that precedes famine declarations and drought-driven crises.
Food price and access shocks are a primary proximate driver of mass protest in low/middle income countries; FIES captures accumulated grievance before a protest tipping point.
Food insecurity is a core component of humanitarian crisis declarations; the FIES measure provides a consistent cross-country quantification of crisis depth.
Food insecurity co-moves with and often precedes broader poverty crises; adds a consumption-access dimension orthogonal to income-based poverty measures.
High food insecurity creates political pressure for social protection reforms; the link is real but indirect and often lagged.

name: Bank nonperforming loans to total gross loans (%)
note: Banking sector health; credit risk indicator
why: Non-performing loan ratios signal latent insolvency stress within the banking system before it erupts into open crisis — high NPLs constrain credit supply, amplify recessions, and can trigger depositor panic and government bailout demands. It provides the balance-sheet deterioration signal that precedes banking crises in the QGI event catalog.
coverage_note: WB WDI; coverage improves markedly after 2000; sparse for low-income and fragile states; some gaps in early 2000s for transition economies.

trends.reason: NPL ratio is the direct balance-sheet precursor of banking crises; among the strongest single predictors in financial distress literature.
High NPLs depress credit and amplify recessions; strong empirical link via credit-growth suppression channel.
Banking stress and currency crises are frequently twin; NPLs add banking-channel signal to macro indicators.
Bank recapitalization pressures force fiscal adjustments; adds financial-sector feedback signal.
Post-liberalization credit booms often generate NPL cycles; marginal orthogonal signal for this Trend.

name: Oil rents (% of GDP)
note: Oil rent share of GDP; petro-state exposure
why: Oil rents as a share of GDP directly quantifies petro-state dependency and the associated vulnerability to commodity price shocks that can trigger fiscal crises, subsidy cuts, and popular unrest when oil revenues collapse. It is a structurally important indicator because it shapes the distribution of political economy incentives — patronage systems, ruling coalition survival, and the rentier bargain.
coverage_note: WB WDI back to 1970 for most producers; non-oil countries report zero (which is valid), so effective signal coverage is narrower (~60-70 countries with non-trivial values).

trends.reason: Direct measurement of oil-revenue centrality to the economy; the strongest single structural predictor for oil sector policy and crisis events.
High oil-rent share creates resource-curse conditions — grievance over distribution, rebel funding, and state fragility from rent shocks.
Oil-rent shocks (price collapses) force emergency fiscal adjustments; this indicator captures the exposure level that makes fiscal policy events likely.
Petro-states show boom-bust GDP cycles tightly linked to oil rent; exposure amplifies recession risk from external price shocks.
Subsidy-cut protests in oil economies are a well-documented transmission channel from rent collapse to social mobilisation.

name: Total natural resources rents (% of GDP)
note: Natural resource dependency; Dutch disease risk
why: Total natural resource rents as a share of GDP measures the degree to which a state's economy and fiscal system depend on extractable resource windfalls — a key driver of Dutch disease, elite rent-seeking, and regime vulnerability to commodity price shocks. Resource-dependent states show systematically different instability pathways (boom-bust, coup risk, secessionism over resource zones).
coverage_note: WB WDI broad coverage from 1970; some micro-states and recent entrants have gaps; rents methodology revised several times so early series may not be fully comparable.

trends.reason: High resource rent dependency is the primary structural precondition for resource-driven conflict; near-definitive feature for this trend.
Total rents (majority oil/gas in most high-dependency states) directly tracks fiscal exposure driving oil-and-gas political events.
Nationalisation events cluster around resource-rich countries when rents shift or external prices spike.
Resource rent dependency increases conflict attractiveness via lootable wealth, funding rebel movements and prolonging wars.

name: Labour income share as a percent of GDP — ILO modelled (%)
note: Wage/labour share of GDP; functional income distribution; SDG 10.4.1 primary input
why: Labour income share as a percent of GDP (ILO modelled) directly measures how national income is distributed between labour and capital; declining labour share signals rising structural inequality, wage repression, and eroding household purchasing power — conditions that build social grievance and fuel mass mobilisation events such as protests, labour actions, and poverty crises. It is the SDG 10.4.1 primary input and provides a distributional lens that GDP-level metrics lack.
coverage_note: ILO modelled estimates extend coverage to ~190 countries but rely on imputation for many developing economies; direct survey-based estimates are available for ~100 countries; modelled values for low-data countries carry higher uncertainty.

trends.reason: Declining labour share is a structural grievance driver; prolonged wage stagnation relative to profit growth historically precedes broad-based protest waves (Arab Spring, Latin American cycles).
Labour share is the distributional measure most directly tied to wage bargaining outcomes; falling share motivates strike and collective action mobilisation.
Labour income share is the primary SDG 10.4 inequality signal; sustained compression of labour share translates directly into poverty and inequality crisis conditions.
Rapid drops in labour share during downturns amplify recessionary consumer demand weakness; useful co-movement signal for economic stress Trends.
Very low labour shares sometimes trigger social policy responses (minimum wage reforms, social transfers); the link is real but episodic and policy-mediated.

name: SDG 2.c.1 Indicator of food price anomalies (IFPA)
note: Food price volatility anomaly indicator; early warning for food price spikes and political instability.
why: The SDG 2.c.1 Indicator of Food Price Anomalies (IFPA) directly measures domestic food price volatility anomalies, flagging periods when prices diverge sharply from international benchmarks — historically a trigger for mass protests and political instability in food-import-dependent countries. As a real-time early-warning index it is action-oriented rather than purely descriptive.
coverage_note: FAOSTAT SDG 2.c.1; coverage limited to countries with sufficient price series data; shorter time series (~2010+) constrains recipe training on early history; benchmark-year or sparse collection in some countries.

trends.reason: Food price spikes are a canonical mass-protest trigger (Arab Spring 2011, bread-riot literature); IFPA anomaly flag likely top-40 entry for protest Trend.
Domestic food price anomalies co-occur with supply shocks from drought; strong mechanistic link to famine-related event onset.
Food price volatility amplifies humanitarian crises; plausible top-40 entry especially in fragile-state contexts.
Price anomalies disproportionately harm low-income households, worsening inequality and deepening poverty; moderate link to crisis events.
Food price shocks can contribute to broader economic stress but causal direction is often reversed (recession causes food insecurity); marginal lift.

name: Prevalence of population unable to afford a healthy diet (% population)
note: Share unable to afford CoHD; demand-side food access gap with income distribution component.
why: The prevalence of inability to afford a healthy diet combines food price levels with household income distributions, making it a demand-side food security indicator that is sensitive to both commodity price shocks and welfare inequality — it directly precedes food-related grievances and can escalate rapidly when prices spike. Unlike production-side metrics, it captures whether populations can actually access adequate food.
coverage_note: FAO Cost of Healthy Diet methodology only became available from 2017; short time series limits recipe walk depth — this is a significant caveat for XGBoost walks requiring multi-year movement shapes. Coverage ~150 countries.

trends.reason: Unaffordability of healthy diet is the closest available proxy to famine access-failure; it directly measures the demand-side food security collapse that characterises famine onset.
Food price grievances are among the strongest empirical predictors of protest onset; unaffordable healthy diet captures the income-price interaction that triggers mobilisation.
Diet unaffordability is a direct outcome measure of poverty and inequality; strongly correlated with income distribution and purchasing power.
Food insecurity at scale is a defining component of humanitarian crises; this indicator contributes a demand-side dimension absent from supply metrics.
Short time series (2017+) and indirect link make this a marginal feature for economic recession; likely below top-40 threshold for this Trend given competition from macro indicators.

name: Urban Slum Population Share (%)
note: Share of urban population living in slums; UN-HABITAT via OWID; urban fragility and inequality signal
why: Urban slum population share measures the concentration of economically marginalised, spatially segregated populations within cities — a well-documented structural precondition for urban unrest, political radicalisation, and grievance-based mass protest, especially where urbanisation outpaces formal employment and service delivery. It also serves as a slow-moving inequality proxy distinct from income-distribution measures.
coverage_note: UN-HABITAT via OWID; coverage strongest for developing-country cities; high-income OECD countries often excluded or near-zero; temporal frequency sparse (census-linked, ~5-year updates); interpolation needed for annual ML features.

trends.reason: Slum share is a direct spatial index of the grievance-dense urban poor who constitute the mobilisation base for large-scale urban protests.
Slum share directly quantifies acute urban poverty; orthogonal to income-based inequality measures and adds housing/services deprivation dimension.
Dense informal settlements provide cover and recruitment for armed groups; slum share correlates with sub-state violent event density in the literature.
High slum share creates political pressure for housing and social policy reforms; secondary signal with moderate empirical support.

name: Executive Corruption Index
note: Executive corruption: bribery, embezzlement, cronyism
why: V-Dem's Executive Corruption Index aggregates expert assessments of executive bribery, embezzlement, and cronyism into a continuous country-year measure, capturing the degree to which executive authority is exercised for private gain rather than public ends. High executive corruption erodes regime legitimacy, distorts resource allocation, and raises the probability of protest, coup, and governance breakdown.
coverage_note: V-Dem full coverage ~180 countries from 1900; expert-coded so no data gaps, but coding quality for authoritarian states with limited observer access may carry higher uncertainty.

trends.reason: Executive Corruption Index is the most direct V-Dem measure of the phenomenon this Trend models; expected to be a top-greedy-selection feature.
Corruption-driven grievances are a leading mobilisation driver; anti-corruption protests are the largest protest category globally across the event dataset.
Corrupt executives typically repress accountability mechanisms; executive corruption and repression are mechanically linked.
Military coups are frequently justified by coup leaders on anti-corruption grounds and occur at elevated rates in high-corruption environments.
Corrupt executives may leverage corruption networks for power consolidation; provides marginal context alongside autocratization indicators.

name: Executive Respects Constitution
note: Executive respects constitutional and judicial constraints
why: V-Dem's executive respects constitution indicator measures whether the head of government abides by constitutional limits and judicial rulings — its decline is the definitional marker of executive power consolidation and the erosion of horizontal accountability that precedes democratic backsliding, institutional purges, and eventually coup or regime change.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal country coverage from 1900; expert-coded with measurement uncertainty intervals; reliable post-1970 for most countries.

trends.reason: This indicator is the direct operational measurement of the executive constitutionalism erosion that defines power consolidation events.
Executives who disrespect existing constitutional constraints are the primary agents of constitutional change events, whether by overreach or forced revision.
Sustained decline in executive constitution-respect is the canonical early indicator of democratic backsliding — a reversal can also signal positive transition.
Constitutional violations by executives sometimes invite counter-coups from institutional actors defending the constitutional order.
Executives who override constitutional constraints typically expand repressive powers beyond legal limits, linking to repression events.

name: Inequality in Income
note: Atkinson measure of income inequality used in IHDI computation; distinct from Gini
why: The Atkinson-based income inequality measure used in the IHDI captures distributional skew that Gini misses at the extremes, and is a known predictor of grievance-driven unrest: societies where income concentration accelerates are more susceptible to populist mobilization, elite-mass conflict, and social instability.
coverage_note: UNDP HDR coverage ~150 countries but survey-dependent — high-income and conflict countries have gaps; annual interpolation used between survey rounds, reducing temporal precision; distinct from GINI so not redundant with WB series.

trends.reason: Direct measure of income inequality that defines this Trend category; strongest theoretical fit.
Empirical literature consistently links rising inequality to protest mobilization; Atkinson measure captures top-tail concentration especially relevant.
Income inequality is a direct driver of wage-dispute strikes and labour mobilisation; captures the distributional grievance.
High pre-existing inequality can amplify recession severity but the reverse channel is stronger; tangential signal.
Corruption and inequality co-evolve but INEQ_INC is an outcome variable not a direct corruption signal.

name: Horizontal Accountability Index
note: V-Dem v2x_horacc — country-year political indicator
why: Horizontal accountability — the capacity of legislatures, judiciaries, and oversight bodies to constrain the executive — is a leading indicator of institutional degradation and authoritarian drift; its decline traces the gradual erosion of checks that precedes coups, power consolidation, and political repression.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal; pre-WWII estimates carry wider uncertainty; most reliable and most relevant for post-1945 democratic contexts.

trends.reason: Declining horizontal accountability is the definitional precursor to executive consolidation — captures the institutional weakening trajectory that precedes this Trend's terminating event.
Weak institutional checks remove constraints on military intervention; horacc decline is an established coup precursor in the literature.
Constitutional rewrites that concentrate power typically track horacc inflections; movement shape alignment plausible.
Weak oversight enables corruption; co-movement provides signal complementary to direct corruption measures.
Accountability institution strengthening is a key marker of genuine democratisation; rising horacc traces transition run-up.

name: Vertical Accountability Index
note: Vertical accountability through elections and parties
why: Vertical Accountability captures the quality of electoral and party-based mechanisms through which citizens can sanction or replace governments — when this deteriorates, incumbents become insulated from voter punishment, correlating strongly with democratic backsliding, electoral violence, and protest-driven instability. Declining vertical accountability is a robust leading indicator of regime change trajectories.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert survey; strong historical coverage; the indicator is most meaningful in competitive political systems — coding exists but has less discriminating power in fully closed autocracies.

trends.reason: Vertical accountability is explicitly constructed from electoral quality components; its decline captures the structural deterioration in electoral integrity that precedes contested or rigged elections.
Both democratization and de-democratization episodes involve measurable shifts in vertical accountability; the indicator captures the trend-level movement shape that precedes transition events.
Consolidation systematically undermines electoral accountability; vertical accountability decline is a measurable, gradual precursor to consolidation events.
When vertical channels (elections) are blocked, citizens substitute with horizontal pressure (protest); declining vertical accountability predicts protest substitution dynamics.
Constitutional changes affecting electoral rules are a tool for manipulating vertical accountability; marginal signal beyond the electoral-specific sub-components.

name: Civil Society Participation Index
note: V-Dem v2x_cspart — country-year political indicator
why: Civil society participation measures the breadth and depth of autonomous citizen organization beyond the state — high participation creates accountability buffers that restrain executive overreach, while a collapse in civil society is a leading indicator of democratic backsliding and repression. It captures the societal resilience dimension that mediates between grievances and political outcomes.
coverage_note: V-Dem standard global coverage; expert-coded composite; more reliable post-1950 as organizational data improves.

trends.reason: Civil society is a primary driver of democratization; strong theoretical and empirical prior for top-40 entry in this Trend.
Civil society organizations are the organizational backbone of protest movements; directly predictive of mobilization capacity.
Civil society suppression IS repression; decline in this index reliably precedes or accompanies repression escalation.
Civil society advocacy drives human rights reform agendas; adds agency-side signal to institutional indicators.
Strong civil society pushes social policy reform but correlation with other governance indicators is high; marginal independent lift.

name: High Court Independence
note: High court independent from executive interference
why: High court independence from executive interference is a foundational institutional variable: when the apex court is captured, it removes the last formal check on executive arbitrariness, enabling a cascade of repression, property rights erosion, and political persecution. Deterioration in this indicator is a measurable early-warning signal that precedes both democratic backsliding and business-climate crises.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-coded; full country-year panel back to 1900 with typical uncertainty caveats for early decades.

trends.reason: Judicial capture is a defining step in the consolidation playbook; this indicator directly measures the variable the Trend predicts.
An executive-compliant court validates mass detentions and political trials; loss of high-court independence enables repression escalation.
Court packing and constitutional court restructuring events are directly indexed by this score; independence drops often co-occur with constitutional change.
Without independent judicial oversight, human rights violations face no domestic remedy; the institutional pathway is well-established in the literature.

name: Executive Oversight by Legislature
note: V-Dem v2lgotovst — country-year political indicator
why: Legislative oversight of the executive is a direct measure of institutional checks on executive power; its erosion is a near-universal precursor to authoritarian consolidation, corruption escalation, and constitutional crises. This indicator adds a horizontal accountability dimension distinct from judicial independence and civil society watchdog indicators.
coverage_note: V-Dem full panel; single-party or zero-legislature periods coded at floor values; coding reliability strongest post-1950.

trends.reason: Declining legislative oversight is a textbook step in executive power consolidation; high theoretical and empirical basis.
Constitutional changes that alter power balances are often preceded and enabled by weakened legislative oversight.
Weak oversight removes the primary institutional brake on executive corruption.
Dysfunctional legislatures create political vacuums that military actors exploit for coup justification.

name: Internet Censorship Effort
note: Government internet censorship effort
why: V-Dem's Internet Censorship Effort measures the degree to which governments actively restrict online information access, a leading indicator of regime efforts to suppress dissent and control political narratives before and during periods of political repression, protests, and democratic backsliding. Spikes in censorship effort often precede or accompany executive crackdowns, making it a valuable early-warning signal across governance and social mobilisation Trends.
coverage_note: V-Dem covers ~180 countries; internet censorship coding starts meaningfully around 2000 when internet penetration became geopolitically relevant; pre-2000 data exists but has low variance and limited signal; expert codings are most reliable post-2010.

trends.reason: Internet censorship is a modern tool of political repression; crackdowns on online speech systematically precede or accompany broader repressive campaigns against civil society.
Autocratizing governments consistently escalate internet controls as they consolidate power; censorship effort rises measurably in the run-up to competitive authoritarianism episodes.

Censorship escalation around protest periods (internet shutdowns, social media blocks) is a documented government response; the variable captures both pre-protest suppression attempts and reactive crackdowns.
Censorship rollback is a common early reform signal in democratic transitions; sustained high censorship distinguishes consolidating autocracies from transitioning states.
Digital rights violations are now formally part of international human rights frameworks; censorship effort captures a systematic rights-denial dimension not covered by physical violence metrics.

name: Foreign Government Domestic Disinformation
note: Foreign governments run domestic disinformation campaigns
why: Measures whether foreign governments run disinformation campaigns targeting the domestic population, capturing information-warfare interference as a distinct channel of foreign meddling separate from military or economic pressure. Rising scores signal externally manufactured political instability particularly relevant to hybrid-warfare and election-interference scenarios.
coverage_note: V-Dem; global coverage but reliable only post-2000 for v2sm* items; expert-survey based so may lag fast-moving information environments by 1-2 years; pre-2008 values near-zero for most countries.

trends.reason: Foreign disinformation campaigns are a primary tool of hybrid warfare and typically co-occur with or precede other forms of foreign intervention; direct mechanistic alignment.
Election interference via disinformation is the most documented use case; high scores predict contested or delegitimized electoral outcomes.
Exposed foreign disinformation operations frequently trigger diplomatic expulsions and ruptures between targeted and perpetrating states.
Governments targeted by foreign disinformation often respond with increased domestic surveillance and repression to counter perceived foreign-backed opposition.
Foreign disinformation frequently amplifies inter-ethnic grievances; marginal contribution where ethnic fault lines already exist.

name: Online Political Polarization of Society
note: Online political polarization causing social fragmentation
why: V-Dem's Online Political Polarisation of Society measures expert-coded assessments of how social media-driven polarisation fragments social cohesion and erodes the centrist space needed for democratic bargaining. Rising polarisation is a pre-radicalisation signal that predicts escalation from online to offline political conflict and is increasingly a leading indicator of democratic erosion and violent unrest.
coverage_note: V-Dem standard coverage; this item was only added once internet/social media became relevant, so reliable data effectively starts around 2000-2005; pre-2000 data should not be used.

trends.reason: Online polarisation both mobilises and radicalises protest participants; strong empirical association with protest wave onset in the 2010s-2020s.
Social polarisation is a consistent upstream condition for political violence escalation; polarisation reduces barriers to viewing violence as legitimate.
Polarisation is a primary mechanism of democratic backsliding — it creates conditions for strongmen to exploit divisions and consolidate power.
Polarising leaders actively cultivate online division as a governance strategy; the indicator may capture both cause and effect of consolidation.
Identity-based social movements are often amplified by online polarisation; plausible but secondary pathway.

name: Anti-System Movements Active
note: Anti-system movements challenging regime
why: Active anti-system movements measure organised societal challenges to regime legitimacy that stop short of armed conflict but signal deep structural rupture — they are a pre-cursor indicator for coups, democratic reversals, and mass violence. QGI values this because it captures the mobilisation phase before terminating events, distinguishing normal opposition from existential challenges to regime continuity.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-coded binary/ordinal; coverage near-universal; anti-system movement coding requires expert judgement so inter-coder reliability varies more than structural indicators.

trends.reason: Anti-system movements are the organised backbone of large protest waves; expected strong top-feature for mass protest Trend.
Anti-system mobilisation creates the political crisis conditions that trigger coup attempts; well-documented empirical link.
Anti-system movements often precede or drive democratisation episodes; plausible but movement outcomes are varied.
Unresolved anti-system mobilisation can escalate to insurgency; useful upstream signal for conflict Trends.

name: Strength of Anti-Regime Sentiment
note: Strength of anti-regime sentiment in population and elites
why: Anti-regime sentiment strength measures the breadth and intensity of opposition to the incumbent regime among both population and elite segments — a direct pre-mobilization signal that captures latent political tension before it erupts into protests, coups, or repression events. It is distinct from formal opposition party strength, capturing diffuse sentiment across society and elite networks.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-coded; near-universal coverage from 1900; annual cadence with good developing-country expert networks.

trends.reason: Anti-regime sentiment is the most direct attitudinal precursor to mass protest mobilization; expected to be a dominant feature for this Trend.
Elite anti-regime sentiment is a necessary condition for coup plotters to build internal support; strong structural link to coup onset.
Sustained high anti-regime sentiment is a structural driver of democratic transitions; well-supported in comparative politics literature.
High anti-regime sentiment provokes pre-emptive executive consolidation to suppress opposition; plausible leading indicator.
Rising anti-regime sentiment triggers repressive responses; the sentiment measure leads the repression measure temporally.

name: Political Regime Type (Regimes of the World, V-Dem RoW)
note: 4-category classification: closed autocracy/electoral autocracy/electoral democracy/liberal democracy; V-Dem RoW 1900-2025; NOT in existing 109
why: The V-Dem Regimes of the World 4-category typology (closed autocracy → liberal democracy) encodes regime-type as a categorical structural variable that conditions almost every political risk mechanism — coup risk, protest dynamics, conflict recurrence, and repression intensity all differ fundamentally across these categories, making regime type one of the most powerful stratifying features in any political-risk model.
coverage_note: Full V-Dem RoW coverage from 1900; OWID-hosted for easy access; treated as ordered categorical or one-hot encoded for XGBoost; essentially complete contemporary coverage.

trends.reason: Coup risk is overwhelmingly concentrated in electoral and closed autocracies; regime type is the single strongest structural predictor of coup occurrence.
Transition events are definitionally moves between regime categories; the current type captures the starting position of every potential transition arc.
Systematic state repression is structurally associated with closed and electoral autocracies; regime type stratifies repression risk sharply.
Consolidation episodes begin in electoral autocracies or eroding democracies; current regime type sets the feasibility and form of consolidation.
Protest scale and state response dynamics differ substantially between regime types; type provides essential context for protest-mobilisation signals.

name: State Capacity Index (Hanson & Sigman)
note: Composite Bayesian latent variable index of coercive+extractive+administrative state capacity; 177 countries 1960-2015; NOT in 109
why: The Hanson & Sigman composite State Capacity Index aggregates coercive, extractive, and administrative sub-dimensions into a single latent variable, capturing the government's ability to govern, tax, and control territory simultaneously. Low state capacity is the structural precondition underlying civil war, coup risk, and governance collapse across multiple Trends.
coverage_note: Series ends at 2015 — a meaningful recency gap; recent events (2016-2024) will be unrepresented, limiting leading-signal utility for current-window predictions. No planned update known.

trends.reason: Low state capacity is the foundational structural precondition for insurgency; the composite index captures the multi-dimensional fragility that enables armed challengers.
Weak administrative and extractive capacity makes civilian governments vulnerable to military displacement; state capacity is among the strongest coup-risk predictors.
Low-capacity states often substitute targeted repression for institutional governance; inverse relationship between capacity and repression intensity.
State capacity directly determines crisis response effectiveness; low-capacity states experience higher humanitarian impact from the same shock magnitude.
State incapacity to mediate inter-group disputes raises communal conflict risk; provides marginal upstream signal.

name: Deadly Electoral Violence Events (count, country-year, from DECO)
note: Count of georeferenced lethal electoral violence events; election-period instability signal distinct from armed conflict
why: Georeferenced lethal electoral violence event counts capture the specific political-competition violence that clusters around electoral cycles — distinct from armed conflict, it signals contested political environments where candidates, parties, and voters face physical coercion, which is a leading indicator of disputed elections, regime delegitimisation, and post-election crisis escalation.
coverage_note: UCDP DECO covers electoral events with documented deaths; many country-years are zeros (non-occurrences); coverage limited to countries with documented electoral violence; ends ~2022 in current release.

trends.reason: Electoral violence directly shapes and precedes contested election events — the count is the most precise leading signal for high-risk electoral periods.
Lethal electoral violence is a specific sub-type of political violence with documented periodicity around electoral cycles.
Electoral violence by incumbents is often a manifestation of broader repression of political competition.
Electoral violence signals disputed legitimacy that complicates post-election government formation and coalition building.

name: Violent Political Protest Deaths (country-year aggregate)
note: Fatalities from violent political protests (below armed conflict threshold); protest repression and political volatility signal
why: Deaths from violent political protests sit below the armed-conflict threshold but above routine demonstrations, marking the inflection zone where state-civilian tension escalates — this sub-conflict violence level is a leading indicator of full conflict onset and political regime instability.
coverage_note: Derived from UCDP GED events classified as political protests with lethal outcomes; available wherever GED has coverage (~145 countries); zero-inflated — peaceful countries will record zero for most years.

trends.reason: Lethal protest events are the direct quantitative measure of violent mobilization defining this Trend; high specificity.
Protest fatalities frequently arise from state repression of demonstrators; strong bidirectional signal.
Sub-conflict lethal protest deaths are a primary component of political violence Trend; near-definitional link.
Protest-driven violence often precedes or accompanies democratization episodes; useful leading signal.
Escalating protest violence is a recognized early-stage conflict escalation signal; moderate predictive value.

name: GED Total Deaths Best Estimate (all types combined, country-year)
note: Aggregate of best-estimate deaths from all GED events (SB+NS+OS) in country-year; total lethality from organized violence
why: Aggregate best-estimate deaths across all organised violence types (state-based, non-state, one-sided) provides the most comprehensive single lethality signal — capturing the full violence environment of a country-year rather than any one conflict type, making it a broad-spectrum conflict intensity feature for QGI recipes.
coverage_note: UCDP GED covers conflict-affected countries only; zero-violence countries absent or coded zero from 1989; pre-1989 not available; data most complete for Africa, Middle East, Asia.

trends.reason: Total deaths aggregate captures civil war intensity trajectory directly; highly likely to be a top greedy feature for this Trend.
Mass casualties are both a cause and core indicator of humanitarian crisis; aggregate deaths provide a strong leading and concurrent signal.
GED includes one-sided violence and non-state conflict deaths from terrorism-adjacent events; aggregate trajectory traces terrorist escalation patterns.
Total organised violence deaths is the broadest direct measure of the phenomenon this Trend captures.
High total lethality thresholds historically trigger foreign intervention; aggregate deaths proxy the severity threshold that prompts external action.

name: State-Based Conflict Onset (binary: new conflict in year, country-year)
note: Binary flag for new conflict onset from UCDP Onset Dataset; leading rather than contemporaneous conflict signal
why: State-Based Conflict Onset is a binary leading indicator specifically coded for new conflict initiation — distinct from ongoing conflict presence — capturing the moment when organized violence crosses the threshold. As a leading rather than contemporaneous signal it is methodologically superior for ML feature engineering in Trends predicting conflict events, avoiding the circularity of using ongoing-conflict flags as predictors of conflict-type events.
coverage_note: UCDP conflict-affected countries only; countries with no conflict history have zero variance — the indicator adds value in the relevant risk-exposed pool; binary, so no scaling issues.

trends.reason: Onset is the most direct structural precursor to civil war — it captures the initiation event before the conflict has accumulated sufficient deaths to dominate other indicators; likely a top greedy feature.
State-based conflict onset encompasses interstate conflict initiation; onset coding precedes intensity escalation, providing a leading signal for interstate war events.
New conflict onset is the formalization of political violence into organized armed activity; captures the threshold-crossing moment most relevant to the political violence Trend.
Conflict onset and coup risk are co-determined by institutional fragility; onset in neighboring contexts also elevates coup probability via regional contagion.
New conflict onset is the primary trigger for acute humanitarian crises; onset coding provides earlier signal than displacement or fatality counts.

name: Years Since Last Active Conflict (country-year, derived)
note: Years elapsed since last UCDP-recorded organized violence above threshold; post-conflict stability duration, recurrence risk proxy
why: Years since last active conflict is a canonical recurrence-risk proxy — post-conflict societies face elevated relapse risk that decays over time, and this derived counter captures the duration of the peace interval that existing conflict intensity measures miss entirely. It adds a temporal memory signal that is mechanistically orthogonal to current violence levels.
coverage_note: Derived from UCDP GED/PRIO-ACD; only covers countries with at least one observed conflict episode; conflict-naive countries require a zero/null treatment convention.

trends.reason: Post-conflict relapse is the dominant pattern in civil war literature; this counter directly encodes recurrence window risk.
Peace processes are triggered by conflict recency; years since conflict is a leading determinant of peace mission deployment.
Sub-threshold violence risks are elevated in the post-conflict window; temporal memory signal unique in the pool.
Foreign interventions cluster in early post-conflict windows; conflict recency is a plausible trigger signal.
Transitional justice mechanisms are deployed in post-conflict periods; years since conflict anchors the timeline.

name: Peace Agreement Signed (binary, country-year, from UCDP PAD)
note: Binary: at least one peace agreement signed in country-year; peace process milestone signal from UCDP Peace Agreement Dataset
why: A binary flag for peace agreement signings captures a discrete institutional milestone in conflict resolution that reshapes the political landscape — creating both opportunities for sustained peace and risks of implementation failure and spoiler violence. As a leading-to-lagging marker it is useful on both sides: post-conflict Trends can be anchored to the agreement date, and the absence of agreements despite prolonged conflict is itself informative.
coverage_note: UCDP PAD covers only conflict-affected countries (by definition); most country-years are zero, which is valid but sparse — effectively a conditional indicator.

trends.reason: Direct measurement of the defining event in this Trend category; agreement signing is the canonical terminating event for armed conflict phases.
Agreement signings follow civil war phases and predict short-term conflict intensity drops; the lead-lag relationship is strong and bidirectional in time-series.
Peace agreements often include transitional justice provisions; signing year is a temporal anchor for accountability-process events.
Failed or stalled agreements can coincide with renewed repression of civil society; marginal signal through the implementation-failure pathway.

name: Refugees by Country of Origin (total stock, end-year)
note: End-year stock of people recognized as refugees originating from each country; core displacement pressure signal
why: End-year stock of refugees originating from each country is a cumulative, internationally-validated measure of how dangerous conditions have become for that country's population — effectively a global consensus judgment on origin-country risk. Stocks respond to conflict onset, political repression, and humanitarian crises and persist as slow-moving structural signals.
coverage_note: UNHCR; near-universal coverage; pre-1990 series sparse for many countries; consistent annual data broadly available from ~1990 onward; near-zero values for stable countries still present in series.

trends.reason: REF_COO is the primary refugee stock measure; definitionally aligned with migration/refugee Trend — near-certain top-40 entry.
Mass refugee production is a hallmark of civil war; refugee stock levels strongly co-vary with civil war duration and intensity.
Refugee stock is a core humanitarian crisis metric reflecting cumulative displacement pressure; likely top-40 entry for this Trend.
Refugee flows from non-conflict states are often driven by political persecution; plausible top-40 entry for repression Trend.
Large refugee stocks signal systematic human rights failures in origin country; moderate lift expected.

name: Stateless Persons (end-year stock)
note: Count of persons without any nationality; indicator of ethnic/citizenship discrimination and governance failure
why: Stateless persons — those with no recognised nationality — signal systematic ethnic, religious, or political discrimination embedded in legal and governance frameworks. Statelessness is both an outcome of past ethnic conflict and a structural driver of future instability, as stateless communities face compound marginalisation that correlates with communal conflict and human rights crisis events.
coverage_note: UNHCR stateless data is highly uneven — it depends on countries actively reporting stateless populations, which many do not; actual global stateless population is estimated at 4M+ but recorded total is ~3.9M across ~90 reporting countries; undercount is severe for Asia (especially South/Southeast Asia) where statelessness is most prevalent.

trends.reason: Statelessness is both a product of ethnic persecution and a structural driver of communal conflict; large stateless populations are a direct precursor signal for this Trend.
Statelessness is definitionally a human rights issue; high stateless populations indicate systematic legal discrimination that is a strong prior for HRV events.
Stateless persons are among the most likely to become refugees when conflict erupts; the indicator adds the discrimination-pathway dimension to displacement models.
States that maintain large stateless populations typically also deploy broader repression against minority groups.
Statelessness contributes to humanitarian vulnerability but is too structurally stable a variable to be a strong leading indicator of acute humanitarian crises.

name: Share of youth not in employment, education or training (NEET) by sex and age (%)
note: NEET rate; SDG 8.6.1 indicator; catches discouraged youth outside all productive activity
why: NEET rate captures the share of youth excluded from all productive activity — the most direct measure of youth marginalisation and a leading indicator of the grievance pool available for protest mobilisation, radicalization, and recruitment into armed groups. Combined with youth-bulge size indicators it creates a two-dimensional youth-risk surface that neither variable alone provides.
coverage_note: ILOSTAT modelled estimates extend coverage to ~165 countries from the 2000s; raw survey data sparser for LICs pre-2005; SDG 8.6.1 custodian series with improving annual updates; sex disaggregation adds optional feature dimension.

trends.reason: NEET youth are the empirically documented mobilisation base for large protest waves; the rate directly measures idle-youth grievance density.
High NEET rates expand the pool available for insurgent recruitment; cross-national studies find NEET a significant onset predictor after controlling for poverty.
NEET is a structural labour-market inequality measure that complements income Gini; captures the non-monetary exclusion dimension of poverty crises.
High NEET signals labour-market dysfunction that politically activates both excluded youth and incumbent workers facing wage competition from informal labour.
Marginal signal: NEET is associated with domestic radicalisation pathways but the link is conditional on ideology and state capacity, reducing direct lift.

name: Cash surplus/deficit (% of GDP)
note: Fiscal cash balance; short-term fiscal health
why: The cash surplus/deficit as a share of GDP measures the government's actual realized fiscal position based on cash flows rather than accrual accounting, providing a more timely indicator of fiscal stress and public finance deterioration. Widening deficits signal reduced fiscal space, increasing government dependence on borrowing that can cascade into currency pressure and austerity-triggered unrest.
coverage_note: Coverage is good for countries with IMF/GFS reporting; many low-income and conflict-affected states have inconsistent or missing series; pre-1995 data are sparse for most developing countries.

trends.reason: Cash fiscal balance is the most direct short-term indicator of fiscal health; sharp deterioration is the primary trigger for fiscal consolidation events.
Fiscal deficits widen automatically in recessions; conversely, austerity-driven deficit cuts deepen downturns; the series captures both the cause and consequence side of recession dynamics.
Persistent deficits requiring monetary financing are a canonical trigger of exchange-rate pressure and currency crises.
Fiscal retrenchment imposed by deficit crises (spending cuts, tax hikes) is a recurring protest mobilization trigger; the fiscal balance trajectory signals the upstream pressure.
Deficit-financing through bank channels raises sovereign-bank feedback risk; provides marginal complementary signal.

name: Civil Liberties Index
note: V-Dem v2x_civlib — country-year political indicator
why: The V-Dem Civil Liberties Index aggregates freedom of movement, religion, expression, association, and personal integrity — its sustained decline traces the broad-front erosion of rights that defines autocratisation trajectories and precedes repression events, protest mobilisation, and eventually regime-changing opposition, making it a high-signal composite for political-risk models.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage with expert-coded measurement; especially reliable post-1970; the composite aggregation smooths individual component noise.

trends.reason: Civil liberties decline is the broad-spectrum signal of repression — the index covers all key dimensions that define repressive political environments.
Civil liberties trajectory is the canonical measure of democratisation and backsliding; used as a definitional component in most transition datasets.
Civil liberties restriction directly indexes the rights violations that define human rights violation events.
Civil liberties erosion both mobilises protest responses and simultaneously constrains protest capacity — the tension creates volatile protest dynamics.
Executive consolidation of power systematically dismantles civil liberties; the index captures the downstream effects of concentration of authority.

name: Freedom of Expression Index
note: V-Dem v2x_freexp — country-year political indicator
why: Freedom of expression captures the information environment available to citizens and opposition actors: its contraction is a hallmark of autocratization and political repression episodes, while its expansion is a necessary precondition for democratic transitions — making it a versatile leading indicator across multiple political risk Trends.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal coverage from 1900; reliable from ~1945 onwards for most countries; microstates and island nations may have thinner expert coverage pre-1990.

trends.reason: Media suppression and speech restriction are definitional elements of repression regimes; direct causal link.
Declining free expression is a canonical early step in autocratization and power consolidation sequences.
Freedom of expression improvements are both a signal and a precondition of democratic opening; useful transition predictor.
Sudden crackdowns on expression can trigger protest mobilization; expanding expression also enables protest coordination.
Press freedom restrictions and speech suppression are core human rights violations; moderate conceptual overlap.

name: Freedom of Association Index
note: V-Dem v2x_frassoc — country-year political indicator
why: Freedom of association — covering rights to form parties, civil society organisations, and trade unions — captures the civic space contraction that precedes and accompanies political repression and executive consolidation; its decline is a more targeted signal than broad civil liberties indices for mobilisation-blocking dynamics.
coverage_note: V-Dem near-universal; pre-1945 coding sparse and expert-estimated; contemporary series (post-1990) most informative for political Trends.

trends.reason: Association rights suppression is a primary mechanism of political repression; directly traces the civic-space closure trajectory that defines this Trend's shape.
Executives consolidating power systematically restrict party competition and civil organisation; declining frassoc co-moves with consolidation trajectory.
Opening of association rights is a leading indicator and enabling condition for democratic transitions; rising scores trace the run-up shape.
Association freedom enables protest organising; restrictions on it shift mobilisation patterns in ways relevant to this Trend's occurrence timing.
Trade union rights are a core sub-component of frassoc; association freedom directly governs labour organising capacity relevant to this Trend.

name: Government Attacks on Judiciary
note: V-Dem v2jupoatck — country-year political indicator
why: Government attacks on the judiciary measure a specifically destabilizing form of institutional erosion — the executive undermining the last formal check on its own behavior. Judicial attacks are a hallmark of autocratization trajectories and correlate with subsequent escalation to broader repression, constitutional manipulation, and loss of rule of law, making this a reliable leading indicator across several political risk Trends.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert survey; global coverage; indicator fires episodically so country-years with attacks are a minority — but the signal is highly discriminating when it does fire.

trends.reason: Judicial attacks systematically accompany or precede broader repression campaigns; the judiciary is typically targeted early in repression escalation to remove legal recourse.
Judicial attacks are a canonical consolidation tool — removing judicial independence is a near-universal step in the executive power consolidation playbook; likely top greedy feature for this Trend.
Executives attacking the judiciary frequently follow up with constitutional changes to formalize their dominance over courts; provides a leading signal for constitutional event windows.
Judicial independence collapse removes the institutional safeguard for human rights; attacks predict subsequent deterioration in human rights protections.
Judicial attacks signal de-democratization trajectories; marginal signal for genuine transition events since it captures the erosion rather than the inflection point itself.

name: Print and Broadcast Media Critical of Government
note: Media criticizes government and reports opposition views
why: Whether print and broadcast media critically cover the government measures the real independence of the fourth estate — beyond formal press freedom, this captures actual editorial behavior, revealing whether journalists exercise accountability or practice self-censorship. It provides a behavioral media-independence signal that complements structural press freedom indices.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-coded; standard global coverage; more reliable in modern era where media environments are better observed.

trends.reason: Media self-censorship under threat is a repression indicator; behavioral signal that leads formal press freedom declines.
Corruption thrives in media silence; critical media is the accountability watchdog — its absence directly enables corruption.
Neutering critical media is a standard consolidation step; behavioral editorial capture precedes formal media takeover.
Media critical of incumbents facilitates democratic transitions; adds information-environment agency signal.
Correlation with other rights/repression variables is high; marginal independent contribution for human rights Trend.

name: Harassment of Journalists
note: Physical harassment/imprisonment of journalists
why: Physical harassment and imprisonment of journalists is a high-specificity indicator of the state's tolerance for information pluralism and its willingness to use coercion to suppress political narratives — capturing a direct repression mechanism rather than a diffuse press-freedom composite. It tends to intensify ahead of elections, coup attempts, and protest crackdowns where controlling the information environment becomes operationally important to incumbents.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert-coded; globally consistent panel; individual event-level accuracy in autocracies may be understated due to hidden repression.

trends.reason: Journalist harassment is a component-level measure of repression targeting information actors; directly indexes the repression event type.
Consolidating executives systematically harass journalists to suppress opposition narratives; this variable captures the information-control arm of power seizure.
Pre-election journalist crackdowns are a documented pattern in electoral autocracies; the score may lead election-integrity deterioration events.
Repression of journalists during protests amplifies grievances and is a contemporaneous signal for protest escalation and state response severity.

name: Government Domestic Disinformation
note: V-Dem v2smgovdom — country-year political indicator
why: Government-run domestic disinformation campaigns are a measurable indicator of information-environment weaponisation — a modern governance failure that undermines electoral integrity, suppresses opposition, and precedes democratic backsliding. As a V-Dem-coded indicator it is available at country-year resolution from 1990 onward, filling a gap not covered by traditional institutional indicators.
coverage_note: V-Dem social media indicators coded from 1990; pre-social-media years reflect offline propaganda proxies so early values require interpretation caution.

trends.reason: State disinformation is a signature tool of executive power consolidation, documented systematically in autocratisation literature.
Government disinformation campaigns peak around elections to suppress opposition and manipulate voter behaviour.
Information repression co-occurs with physical repression as complementary tools of political control.
Intensified disinformation can both suppress and — when publics detect manipulation — trigger reactive protest mobilisation.

name: Arrests for Online Political Content
note: Arrests of individuals for online political speech
why: V-Dem's Arrests for Online Political Content measures government use of detention and arrest specifically targeting individuals for online speech, capturing an intensifying form of digital repression that directly chills civil society mobilisation and political dissent; it is a leading rather than lagging indicator because arrests for speech typically precede broader crackdowns, making it particularly valuable for run-up detection in repression, protest, and autocratization Trends.
coverage_note: V-Dem expert codings cover ~180 countries; online arrest variable is most reliable post-2010 as social media became politically relevant; pre-2010 values reflect early internet-era blogger arrests and have lower cross-expert agreement; signal is sparse for very closed states where arrests may be underreported to outside experts.

trends.reason: Online political arrests are a direct and systematic repression tactic; escalation of this variable is a documented precursor to broader physical crackdowns on civil society and opposition.
Autocratizing regimes systematically escalate digital repression as part of power consolidation; the variable captures the information-control dimension of authoritarian deepening.
Arrests of online organisers ahead of protest mobilisation are a documented suppression pattern; the variable captures both pre-emptive repression and reactive crackdowns on protest coordination.
Detention for speech is a core civil liberties violation; the variable adds a digital-rights dimension to the human rights violation Trend that physical violence metrics underweight.

Declining arrest rates for online content is a modest liberalisation signal in democratic transition contexts, but the variable's primary utility is in detecting autocratization rather than transition.

name: Freedom of Peaceful Assembly
note: Citizens can freely assemble for protests and meetings
why: Freedom of peaceful assembly is a direct civil-liberties indicator measuring whether citizens can freely gather for protests and political meetings; restrictions on assembly are an early-stage precursor to mass protest escalation and a marker of political repression that often precedes broader human rights deterioration.
coverage_note: V-Dem; global coverage from 1900; expert-survey methodology provides consistent coding across regime types; high confidence for post-1990 data across all regions.

trends.reason: Assembly restrictions are both a direct antecedent and co-occurring feature of protest events; very likely top-40 entry with strong directional signal.
Banning or restricting assemblies is a canonical repression tool; near-certain top-40 entry for political repression Trend.
Assembly freedom is a core human rights dimension; plausible top-40 entry as part of a civil liberties indicator cluster.
Democratization events are associated with expanding assembly rights; indicator likely captures both the run-up and consolidation phases of transitions.
Assembly rights affect workers' ability to strike and organize collectively; marginal lift as labor action has more direct predictors.

name: State of Emergency Declared
note: State of emergency declared restricting civil liberties
why: Declaration of a state of emergency represents an executive's formal invocation of emergency powers that suspend normal constitutional constraints — it is both a symptom of acute political crisis and a tool of repression that can escalate instability. As an event-coded V-Dem variable it captures a discrete legal threshold-crossing that is rare enough to have strong signal value.
coverage_note: V-Dem standard coverage; reliable for post-1945; effective QGI window ~1970-2024. Binary nature means the variable is sparse in stable periods, which is informative but may limit predictive utility in non-crisis baselines.

trends.reason: State of emergency is the most commonly used legal instrument for mass repression; declaring one is both a signal of ongoing repression and an enabler of escalation.
Emergency declarations are a primary mechanism through which executives consolidate power; they frequently precede or accompany constitutional power grabs.
SOE declarations both respond to mass protests and frequently trigger renewed protest by activating opposition; bidirectional signal with strong contemporaneous correlation.
Emergency declarations sometimes precede or accompany coup attempts as competing actors contest executive authority under emergency conditions.
Governments fighting insurgencies frequently declare emergencies; the variable may be contemporaneous rather than leading for this Trend.

name: State-Based Conflict Battle Deaths — Best Estimate (country-year aggregate)
note: Best-estimate battle-related deaths from state-based conflicts aggregated to country-year; core conflict intensity metric
why: Best-estimate battle deaths from state-based conflicts is the gold-standard measure of conflict intensity, capturing the lethality of organised state-vs-armed-group or inter-state violence in a single comparable metric. QGI's conflict Trends benefit from this as a contemporaneous intensity anchor that also carries strong predictive power for sustained conflict duration, peace-process timing, and foreign intervention triggers.
coverage_note: UCDP GED/PRIO-ACD covers all country-years with active state-based conflict from 1989; non-conflict countries are coded zero; coverage is comprehensive for conflict cases but the series is sparse before 1989.

trends.reason: Battle death count is the definitional core metric for civil war intensity; expected top feature for this Trend.
State-based deaths include inter-state conflict fatalities; one of the most direct indicators for the interstate war Trend.
High battle death counts are the primary threshold trigger for international intervention decisions; strong leading signal.
Battle death magnitude shapes the timing and form of peace processes; useful contextual feature.
High battle deaths co-move with civilian displacement and humanitarian need; complementary to displacement-specific indicators.

name: GED Civilian Deaths Best Estimate (all violence types, country-year)
note: Sum of deaths_civilians across all GED events in country-year; direct civilian harm signal from all organized violence
why: GED civilian deaths aggregate best-estimate fatalities across all organized violence types (state-based, non-state, one-sided) for a country-year — uniquely capturing direct civilian harm from the full spectrum of violence rather than just combatant casualties. This is the most comprehensive lethality measure for civilian populations and captures deliberate targeting patterns diagnostic of atrocity and repression events.
coverage_note: UCDP GED covers conflict-affected countries 1989-2023; zero-inflated but informative zeros for peaceful countries; sparse for low-violence years in otherwise active regions.

trends.reason: Civilian fatalities from organized violence are the most direct quantitative measure of severe human rights violations; expected top-feature.
GED civilian deaths aggregate all organized violence types targeting civilians; definitionally central to this Trend.
Civilian casualty levels are a primary indicator of civil war intensity; civilian-specific deaths distinguish deliberate targeting from collateral harm.
